papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs use shared internal circuitry for similar syntactic processes across languages, even in independently trained monolingual models, and employ language-specific components (e.g., feed-forward networks) for language-specific morphological processes.
papers.conclusion: The paper finds that cross-lingual structural similarity is represented within LLMs using shared circuits that invoke the same algorithm independent of language, and that language-specific processing is localized to play a causal role only in languages that require it.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual models use a single circuit to handle the same syntactic process independently of the language in which it occurs.
Monolingual models trained independently on English and Chinese each adopt nearly the same circuit for the IOI task, suggesting consistency in how LLMs learn to handle this aspect of language modeling.
For tasks requiring language-specific morphological processes (e.g., past tense marking in English), multilingual models invoke a largely overlapping circuit but employ language-specific components as needed, such as feed-forward networks in English only for morphological marking.
The circuits identified for the IOI task align with prior work, indicating that the same mechanism is shared between English and Chinese within a multilingual model.
Heads specifically responsible for past tense disambiguation are activated in English but not in Chinese, and they suppress present-tense verbs in English.
papers.limitation: Results are limited to specific tasks and datasets, requiring future work for replication and generalization.
future_direction: Replicate and generalize findings to more tasks and datasets.
Explore cross-disciplinary collaborations to gain fresh perspectives on linguistic universality using LLMs.
Investigate whether circuit overlap can be exploited for improving cross-lingual transfer and safety.
papers.abstract: We employ new tools from mechanistic interpretability in order to ask whether the internal structure of large language models (LLMs) shows correspondence to the linguistic structures which underlie the languages on which they are trained. In particular, we ask (1) when two languages employ the same morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using shared internal circuitry? and (2) when two languages require different morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using different internal circuitry? Using English and Chinese multilingual and monolingual models, we analyze the internal circuitry involved in two tasks. We find evidence that models employ the same circuit to handle the same syntactic process independently of the language in which it occurs, and that this is the case even for monolingual models trained completely independently. Moreover, we show that multilingual models employ language-specific components (attention heads and feed-forward networks) when needed to handle linguistic processes (e.g., morphological marking) that only exist in some languages. Together, our results provide new insights into how LLMs trade off between exploiting common structures and preserving linguistic differences when tasked with modeling multiple languages simultaneously.

papers.title: Tracing Multilingual Representations in LLMs with Cross-Layer Transcoders
papers.research_question: Do multilingual LLMs form shared representations across languages with language-specific decoding, and why does performance favor the dominant training language such as English?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual LLMs form a shared language-agnostic representation space in middle layers, with language-specific decoding in late layers; performance gaps are mechanistically explained by tokenizer bias and feature strength differences.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual LLMs use shared representations in middle layers and language-specific decoding in late layers, with performance gaps explained by feature strength and tokenizer bias.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual LLMs consistently form a shared language-agnostic space in middle layers, regardless of English dominance in training data.
Language-specific decoding depends on a small set of high-frequency features in late layers that linearly encode language identity from early layers.
Non-English performance failures are linked to dim late-layer features, weak middle-layer clusters, and tokenizer bias forcing early layers to specialize in word reassembly.
Finetuning strengthens these features and their connections, improving token assembly and language-specific decoding.
The shared multilingual space emerges as an architectural property, even when models are trained without English.
papers.abstract: Multilingual Large Language Models (LLMs) can process many languages, yet how they internally represent this diversity remains unclear. Do they form shared multilingual representations with language-specific decoding, and if so, why does performance favor the dominant training language? To address this, we train models on different multilingual mixtures and analyze their internal mechanisms using Cross-Layer Transcoders (CLTs) and Attribution Graphs. Our results reveal multilingual shared representations: the model employs highly similar features across languages, while language-specific decoding emerges in later layers. Training models without English shows identical multilingual shared space structures. Decoding relies partly on a small set of high-frequency features in the final layers, which linearly encode language identity from early layers. Intervening on these features allows one language to be suppressed and another substituted. Finally, to explain non-English failures, we perform a Model-Diffing experiment: underperformance arises from dim late-layer features, weak middle-layer clusters, and tokenizer bias toward English that forces early layers to specialize in word reassembly. Finetuning strengthens these features and their links, improving token assembly and language-specific decoding, providing a mechanistic explanation for multilingual gaps. Our models and CLTs are available at https://huggingface.co/collections/CausalNLP/multilingual-clts and https://huggingface.co/collections/CausalNLP/multilingual-gpt2-models. Our code is available at: https://github.com/abirharrasse/MultilingualCLTs

papers.title: Do Large Language Models Think Like the Brain? Sentence-Level Evidences from Layer-Wise Embeddings and fMRI
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether the similarity between LLM representations and human brain activity is due to model scaling or deeper alignment with human language processing principles.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that instruction tuning and semantic comprehension ability, rather than model scale alone, drive the alignment between LLM representations and human brain activity during sentence processing.
papers.conclusion: Instruction tuning and semantic comprehension capacity, not merely parameter size, are key drivers of neural similarity, and the alignment is anatomically and functionally specific to intermediate layers and hemispheric specializations.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate layers of LLMs show higher correlation with brain activity than final layers.
Instruction-tuned models exhibit better performance and stronger neural alignment compared to their base versions.
Hemispheric asymmetry in brain regions aligns with functional specialization, with left-hemisphere regions correlating more with core language processing and right-hemisphere regions with higher cognitive functions.
future_direction: Training procedures that explicitly target alignment with brain data to produce more cognitively plausible models.
Developing hybrid neuro-symbolic LLMs to better reflect distributed and lateralized processing patterns observed in the brain.
papers.abstract: Understanding whether large language models (LLMs) and the human brain converge on similar computational principles remains a fundamental and important question in cognitive neuroscience and AI. Do the brain-like patterns observed in LLMs emerge simply from scaling, or do they reflect deeper alignment with the architecture of human language processing? This study focuses on the sentence-level neural mechanisms of language models, systematically investigating how layer-wise representations in LLMs align with the dynamic neural responses during human sentence comprehension. By comparing hierarchical embeddings from 14 publicly available LLMs with fMRI data collected from participants, who were exposed to a naturalistic narrative story, we constructed sentence-level neural prediction models to identify the model layers most significantly correlated with brain region activations. Results show that improvements in model performance drive the evolution of representational architectures toward brain-like hierarchies, particularly achieving stronger functional and anatomical correspondence at higher semantic abstraction levels. These findings advance our understanding of the computational parallels between LLMs and the human brain, highlighting the potential of LLMs as models for human language processing.

papers.title: Language Arithmetics: Towards Systematic Language Neuron Identification and Manipulation
papers.research_question: How do language-specific neurons in multilingual LLMs control language behavior, and can they be manipulated to steer model outputs across languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces language arithmetics, an additive neuron intervention method, to identify and manipulate language-specific neurons in multilingual LLMs, showing that it can steer language generation and improve performance on downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: Our large-scale study demonstrates that language-specific neurons encode meaningful linguistic features that can be identified, analyzed, and manipulated to steer model behavior across languages. By employing a novel additive intervention method, we show that activating these neurons allows for generation language control and improves performance on various multilingual tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Language-specific neurons cluster in deeper layers, with non-Latin scripts showing greater specialization.
Related languages share overlapping neurons, reflecting linguistic proximity.
Additive language arithmetics outperforms replacement-based methods for language forcing.
Activating target-language neurons improves performance on multilingual tasks like translation, QA, comprehension, and NLI.
Models exhibit internal 'fallback' mechanisms for language selection when dominant language neurons are deactivated.
papers.limitation:
Broader evaluation across more diverse downstream settings is needed.
Quality and fluency of forced outputs across languages, especially low-resource ones, remain underexplored.
Analysis focuses on isolated neurons, overlooking distributed representations and circuits.
Computational constraints limited some experiments to smaller models.
future_direction: Investigate the interactions and dependencies between neurons to understand network-level mechanisms supporting multilingual processing.
More detailed investigation of language fallback dynamics.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong multilingual abilities, yet the neural mechanisms behind language-specific processing remain unclear. We analyze language-specific neurons in Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-Nemo-12B, and Aya-Expanse-8B & 32B across 21 typologically diverse languages, identifying neurons that control language behavior. Using the Language Activation Probability Entropy (LAPE) method, we show that these neurons cluster in deeper layers, with non-Latin scripts showing greater specialization. Related languages share overlapping neurons, reflecting internal representations of linguistic proximity. Through language arithmetics, i.e. systematic activation addition and multiplication, we steer models to deactivate unwanted languages and activate desired ones, outperforming simpler replacement approaches. These interventions effectively guide behavior across five multilingual tasks: language forcing, translation, QA, comprehension, and NLI. Manipulation is more successful for high-resource languages, while typological similarity improves effectiveness. We also demonstrate that cross-lingual neuron steering enhances downstream performance and reveal internal "fallback" mechanisms for language selection when neurons are progressively deactivated. Our code is made publicly available at https://github.com/d-gurgurov/Language-Neurons-Manipulation.

papers.title: The Emergence of Abstract Thought in Large Language Models Beyond Any Language
papers.research_question: Do LLMs think in the distinct space of each language, or do they operate in a higher-level language-agnostic space beyond any specific language? Does the trend of non-English performance compared to English indicate the emergence of abstract thought within LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs progressively develop a core language-agnostic parameter space (shared neurons) that underlies generalization across languages and supports abstract thought. Based on this, neuron-specific training strategies are proposed to enhance multilingual capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Shared neurons form a compact, language-agnostic set that supports abstract reasoning across languages, and neuron-specific training strategies can enhance multilingual performance.
papers.key_findings:
The proportion of language-shared neurons increases with model evolution and correlates with multilingual ability.
Language-shared neurons become more functionally important than language-exclusive neurons, evolving into language-agnostic neurons that support abstract thought.
Neuron-targeted training based on the language-agnostic score effectively improves multilingual performance, with different strategies for models at different developmental stages.
papers.limitation: Limited by computational resources, restricting evaluation on larger LLMs and full exploration of neuron-centric training at larger scales.
future_direction: Evaluation on larger LLMs and exploration of neuron-centric training at larger scales.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) continue to advance, their capacity to function effectively across a diverse range of languages has shown marked improvement. Preliminary studies observe that the hidden activations of LLMs often resemble English, even when responding to non-English prompts. This has led to the widespread assumption that LLMs may "think" in English. However, more recent results showing strong multilingual performance, even surpassing English performance on specific tasks in other languages, challenge this view. In this work, we find that LLMs progressively develop a core language-agnostic parameter space-a remarkably small subset of parameters whose deactivation results in significant performance degradation across all languages. This compact yet critical set of parameters underlies the model's ability to generalize beyond individual languages, supporting the emergence of abstract thought that is not tied to any specific linguistic system. Specifically, we identify language-related neurons-those are consistently activated during the processing of particular languages, and categorize them as either shared (active across multiple languages) or exclusive (specific to one). As LLMs undergo continued development over time, we observe a marked increase in both the proportion and functional importance of shared neurons, while exclusive neurons progressively diminish in influence. These shared neurons constitute the backbone of the core language-agnostic parameter space, supporting the emergence of abstract thought. Motivated by these insights, we propose neuron-specific training strategies tailored to LLMs' language-agnostic levels at different development stages. Experiments across diverse LLM families support our approach.

papers.title: Neuron Specialization: Leveraging intrinsic task modularity for multilingual machine translation
papers.research_question: How do neurons in multilingual translation models exhibit language-specific modularity, and can this be leveraged to reduce interference and improve translation performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that FFN neurons in multilingual models exhibit language-specific modularity, and introduces Neuron Specialization, a method that leverages this to reduce interference and improve translation performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that intrinsic modularity in multilingual models can be leveraged to improve translation performance by reducing interference and enhancing transfer, with Neuron Specialization providing consistent gains.
papers.key_findings:
FFN neurons in multilingual translation models activate in a language-specific way, with overlaps indicating linguistic proximity.
The specialization of neurons evolves across layers, becoming more language-agnostic in the encoder and more specific in the decoder.
The proposed Neuron Specialization method, which updates task-specific neurons via sparse networks, consistently improves translation quality over baselines.
This method effectively reduces negative interference in high-resource languages and boosts knowledge transfer in low-resource languages.
Neuron Specialization is efficient, requiring minimal extra parameters and time compared to adapter-based methods.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to multilingual machine translation and does not explore other multilingual NLP tasks.
Analysis is confined to feed-forward network components, excluding other Transformer elements like attention mechanisms.
Neuron identification relies on ReLU activation states; other activation functions like GELU are not considered.
future_direction: Extend the exploration to a broader range of Multilingual Natural Language Processing tasks beyond translation.
Investigate the modularity of other Transformer components such as attention mechanisms or layer normalization.
Explore neuron specialization for FFNs using activation functions other than ReLU, such as GELU.
papers.abstract: Training a unified multilingual model promotes knowledge transfer but inevitably introduces negative interference. Language-specific modeling methods show promise in reducing interference. However, they often rely on heuristics to distribute capacity and struggle to foster cross-lingual transfer via isolated modules. In this paper, we explore intrinsic task modularity within multilingual networks and leverage these observations to circumvent interference under multilingual translation. We show that neurons in the feed-forward layers tend to be activated in a language-specific manner. Meanwhile, these specialized neurons exhibit structural overlaps that reflect language proximity, which progress across layers. Based on these findings, we propose Neuron Specialization, an approach that identifies specialized neurons to modularize feed-forward layers and then continuously updates them through sparse networks. Extensive experiments show that our approach achieves consistent performance gains over strong baselines with additional analyses demonstrating reduced interference and increased knowledge transfer.

papers.title: Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English?
papers.research_question: Do multilingual LLMs perform key reasoning steps in a representation space closest to English, regardless of input and output languages?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual LLMs perform semantic reasoning in a representation space biased towards English, even for non-English inputs and outputs, as evidenced by logit lens analysis and more effective steering with English-derived vectors.
papers.conclusion: Semantic decisions in LLMs are predominantly made in a representation space close to English, while non-lexical words are processed in the prompt language, and this behavior varies across models.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs route lexical words through English representation space before translating to the target language, while non-lexical words are not necessarily routed through English.
Steering non-English prompts is more effective using English steering vectors than vectors derived from the target language.
Facts are encoded in similar layers across languages, but models have a propensity to answer in English.
The degree of English-routing varies with model multilingualism and size, with more multilingual models routing less through English.
The latent representation structure allows interpolation between facts expressed in different languages while maintaining correctness, indicating shared semantic representations with language-specific components.
papers.limitation:
Tokenization varies across languages, complicating cross-lingual comparisons.
Models may have language confidence and confusion, affecting analysis.
Interpretability methods like steering depend on prompt steerability and may push activations outside the expected distribution.
Alternative methods like sparse autoencoders were not explored due to computational constraints.
future_direction: Developing more robust evaluation procedures for interpretability methods.
Exploring alternative methods like sparse autoencoders for cross-lingual analysis.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have multilingual capabilities and can solve tasks across various languages. However, we show that current LLMs make key decisions in a representation space closest to English, regardless of their input and output languages. Exploring the internal representations with a logit lens for sentences in French, German, Dutch, and Mandarin, we show that the LLM first emits representations close to English for semantically-loaded words before translating them into the target language. We further show that activation steering in these LLMs is more effective when the steering vectors are computed in English rather than in the language of the inputs and outputs. This suggests that multilingual LLMs perform key reasoning steps in a representation that is heavily shaped by English in a way that is not transparent to system users.

papers.title: Mechanistic Understanding and Mitigation of Language Confusion in English-Centric Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does language confusion arise mechanistically in English-centric LLMs, and can it be mitigated through neuron-level interventions?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides the first mechanistic interpretability study of language confusion in LLMs, revealing that confusion points arise from transition failures in final layers and can be effectively mitigated by editing a small set of critical neurons identified through comparative analysis.
papers.conclusion: This work provides the first mechanistic interpretability account of language confusion in English-centric LLMs, demonstrating that targeted neuron editing can robustly mitigate confusion without sacrificing general competence or fluency.
papers.key_findings:
Confusion points are critical drivers of language confusion, and token replacement at these points reduces confusion.
Layer-wise analysis shows that language confusion is caused by failed transitions to the target language in the final layers.
Neuron-level analysis identifies specific FFN neurons in late layers that are responsible for confusion points.
Comparative importance selection of neurons enables effective mitigation of language confusion through editing.
Neuron editing achieves confusion reduction comparable to multilingual tuning for many languages while preserving general competence and output quality.
papers.limitation:
Analysis primarily focuses on the monolingual setting; cross-lingual contexts are left for future research.
Neuron editing interventions may require further validation across broader domains and model architectures.
Fully understanding how these mechanisms interact with other multilingual phenomena warrants further investigation.
future_direction: Extending analysis to cross-lingual contexts
Validating neuron editing across broader domains and model architectures
Investigating interactions with other multilingual phenomena
papers.abstract: Language confusion -- where large language models (LLMs) generate unintended languages against the user's need -- remains a critical challenge, especially for English-centric models. We present the first mechanistic interpretability (MI) study of language confusion, combining behavioral benchmarking with neuron-level analysis. Using the Language Confusion Benchmark (LCB), we show that confusion points (CPs) -- specific positions where language switches occur -- are central to this phenomenon. Through layer-wise analysis with TunedLens and targeted neuron attribution, we reveal that transition failures in the final layers drive confusion. We further demonstrate that editing a small set of critical neurons, identified via comparative analysis with a multilingual-tuned counterpart, substantially mitigates confusion while largely preserving general competence and fluency. Our approach matches multilingual alignment in confusion reduction for many languages and yields cleaner, higher-quality outputs. These findings provide new insights into the internal dynamics of LLMs and highlight neuron-level interventions as a promising direction for robust, interpretable multilingual language modeling. Code and data are available at: https://github.com/ercong21/lang_confusion.

papers.title: Are Knowledge and Reference in Multilingual Language Models Cross-Lingually Consistent?
papers.research_question: Do multilingual language models recall factual knowledge for coreferential statements in a similar manner across languages, how does the mechanism work, and which factors prevent model consistency in multilingual settings?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes cross-lingual consistency of factual knowledge in multilingual models, identifying bottlenecks related to language characteristics and showing that explicit cross-lingual supervision (code-switching, word alignment) improves consistency more than scaling or instruction tuning.
papers.conclusion: The study highlights limitations in cross-lingual consistency of multilingual models and emphasizes the value of explicit cross-lingual alignment supervision and code-switching strategies for enhancing consistency.
papers.key_findings:
Cross-lingual consistency is lower for languages dissimilar to English in script, family, or geography.
A consistency bottleneck exists in specific middle layers of the models.
Vocabulary expansion offers only slight consistency improvements and relies on deep semantic alignment rather than shared scripts.
Code-switching training and cross-lingual word alignment objectives significantly improve consistency, while instruction tuning offers limited gains.
Activation patching on feed-forward neurons based on IG2 scores can partially calibrate consistency at test time, showing a causal relationship.
papers.abstract: Cross-lingual consistency should be considered to assess cross-lingual transferability, maintain the factuality of the model knowledge across languages, and preserve the parity of language model performance. We are thus interested in analyzing, evaluating, and interpreting cross-lingual consistency for factual knowledge. To facilitate our study, we examine multiple pretrained models and tuned models with code-mixed coreferential statements that convey identical knowledge across languages. Interpretability approaches are leveraged to analyze the behavior of a model in cross-lingual contexts, showing different levels of consistency in multilingual models, subject to language families, linguistic factors, scripts, and a bottleneck in cross-lingual consistency on a particular layer. Code-switching training and cross-lingual word alignment objectives show the most promising results, emphasizing the worthiness of cross-lingual alignment supervision and code-switching strategies for both multilingual performance and cross-lingual consistency enhancement. In addition, experimental results suggest promising result for calibrating consistency in the test time via activation patching.

papers.title: Large Language Models Share Representations of Latent Grammatical Concepts Across Typologically Diverse Languages
papers.research_question: In this work, we explore the extent to which LLMs share representations of morphosyntactic concepts such as grammatical number, gender, and tense across languages.
papers.core_contribution: Our findings suggest that even models trained predominantly on English data can develop robust, cross-lingual abstractions of morphosyntactic concepts.
papers.conclusion: Large language models share representations of morphosyntactic concepts across typologically diverse languages, suggesting that they develop cross-lingual abstractions, even when trained primarily on English.
papers.key_findings:
Representations of morphosyntactic concepts are shared across languages, with significant overlap in the top features encoding grammatical categories.
Probing classifiers crucially rely on multilingual features to predict morphosyntactic concepts; ablating multilingual features drops performance to near-chance.
Intervening on single multilingual features can change model behavior in machine translation tasks, demonstrating their causal role.
Interventions are selective, primarily affecting the targeted concept without interfering with other concepts.
Sparse autoencoder features are human-interpretable and activate on relevant grammatical concepts across languages.
papers.limitation:
Distinction between model understanding and generation; some features with high causal effect on probes do not necessarily affect generation.
Human biases in feature interpretation; human explanations of features may be biased and suboptimal.
Sparse autoencoders only recover linearly encoded features; non-linearly encoded concepts may not be captured.
papers.abstract: Human bilinguals often use similar brain regions to process multiple languages, depending on when they learned their second language and their proficiency. In large language models (LLMs), how are multiple languages learned and encoded? In this work, we explore the extent to which LLMs share representations of morphsyntactic concepts such as grammatical number, gender, and tense across languages. We train sparse autoencoders on Llama-3-8B and Aya-23-8B, and demonstrate that abstract grammatical concepts are often encoded in feature directions shared across many languages. We use causal interventions to verify the multilingual nature of these representations; specifically, we show that ablating only multilingual features decreases classifier performance to near-chance across languages. We then use these features to precisely modify model behavior in a machine translation task; this demonstrates both the generality and selectivity of these feature's roles in the network. Our findings suggest that even models trained predominantly on English data can develop robust, cross-lingual abstractions of morphosyntactic concepts.

papers.title: How Do Multilingual Language Models Remember Facts?
papers.research_question: How do factual recall mechanisms in English LLMs generalize to multilingual LLMs, and when does language play a role in recall?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that factual recall mechanisms in multilingual LLMs share similarities with English LLMs but with key differences, such as the role of MLPs in extraction and the composition of relation and language in the last token's function vector.
papers.conclusion: These insights reveal unique mechanisms in multilingual LLMs for recalling information, highlighting the need for new methodologies—such as knowledge evaluation, fact editing, and knowledge acquisition—that are specifically tailored for multilingual LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Previously identified recall mechanisms in English largely apply to multilingual contexts, with nuances based on language and architecture.
Subject enrichment is language-independent, while object extraction is language-dependent.
The last token representation acts as a Function Vector (FV), encoding both the language of the query and the content to be extracted.
In decoder-only LLMs, FVs compose relation and language in two separate stages.
MLPs play a more prominent role in extraction in multilingual LLMs compared to English LLMs.
papers.limitation: Excluded languages with too few examples, limiting the analysis to a subset of languages.
future_direction: Developing new methodologies for knowledge evaluation, fact editing, and knowledge acquisition tailored for multilingual LLMs
Studying whether models 'think' in English by examining how the function vector is altered across languages
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) store and retrieve vast amounts of factual knowledge acquired during pre-training. Prior research has localized and identified mechanisms behind knowledge recall; however, it has only focused on English monolingual models. The question of how these mechanisms generalize to non-English languages and multilingual LLMs remains unexplored. In this paper, we address this gap by conducting a comprehensive analysis of three multilingual LLMs. First, we show that previously identified recall mechanisms in English largely apply to multilingual contexts, with nuances based on language and architecture. Next, through patching intermediate representations, we localize the role of language during recall, finding that subject enrichment is language-independent, while object extraction is language-dependent. Additionally, we discover that the last token representation acts as a Function Vector (FV), encoding both the language of the query and the content to be extracted from the subject. Furthermore, in decoder-only LLMs, FVs compose these two pieces of information in two separate stages. These insights reveal unique mechanisms in multilingual LLMs for recalling information, highlighting the need for new methodologies -- such as knowledge evaluation, fact editing, and knowledge acquisition -- that are specifically tailored for multilingual LLMs.

papers.title: Unraveling Babel: Exploring Multilingual Activation Patterns of LLMs and Their Applications
papers.research_question: How do the internal neuron activation patterns of LLMs differ when processing different languages, and how can these patterns be leveraged for applications like model pruning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to convert dense LLMs into fine-grained MoE architectures to study multilingual activation patterns, and uses these patterns to guide language-specific model pruning, reducing computation while maintaining or even improving performance.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals multilingual activation patterns in LLMs, their connections to language families and instruction tuning, and provides a new effective approach for model pruning and sparse activation.
papers.key_findings:
Activation patterns differ across languages and correlate with language families and genera.
Multilingual shared experts are concentrated in middle layers, while shallow and deep layers contain more language-specific experts.
Instruction tuning significantly alters activation patterns, with the largest changes in the last layer.
Pruning based on expert activation frequency outperforms random pruning and can exceed the performance of the original unpruned model in some languages.
Different layers exhibit different activation sparsity, so configuring layer-specific pruning rates yields better results.
papers.limitation:
The pruning ratio is limited due to low activation sparsity in most layers of models like Llama 2.
There is a concern that simplified representations may fail to capture the model's out-of-distribution behavior, though evaluation on out-of-distribution tasks provides some mitigation.
future_direction: Extend experiments to a broader array of models and languages.
Explore how to further leverage these insights to utilize and enhance the multilingual capabilities of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Recently, large language models (LLMs) have achieved tremendous breakthroughs in the field of NLP, but still lack understanding of their internal neuron activities when processing different languages. We designed a method to convert dense LLMs into fine-grained MoE architectures, and then visually studied the multilingual activation patterns of LLMs through expert activation frequency heatmaps. Through comprehensive experiments on different model families, different model sizes, and different variants, we analyzed the similarities and differences in the internal neuron activation patterns of LLMs when processing different languages. Specifically, we investigated the distribution of high-frequency activated experts, multilingual shared experts, whether multilingual activation patterns are related to language families, and the impact of instruction tuning on activation patterns. We further explored leveraging the discovered differences in expert activation frequencies to guide sparse activation and pruning. Experimental results demonstrated that our method significantly outperformed random expert pruning and even exceeded the performance of unpruned models in some languages. Additionally, we found that configuring different pruning rates for different layers based on activation level differences could achieve better results. Our findings reveal the multilingual processing mechanisms within LLMs and utilize these insights to offer new perspectives for applications such as sparse activation and model pruning.

papers.title: Large Reasoning Models Are (Not Yet) Multilingual Latent Reasoners
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) achieve strong performance on mathematical reasoning tasks, often attributed to their capability to generate explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) explanations. However, recent work shows that LRMs often arrive at the correct answer before completing these textual reasoning steps, indicating the presence of latent reasoning -- internal, non-verbal computation encoded in hidden states. While this phenomenon has been explored in English, its multilingual behavior remains largely unknown. In this paper, we conduct a systematic investigation of multilingual latent reasoning in LRMs across 11 languages. Using a truncation-based strategy, we examine how the correct answer emerges as the model is given only partial reasoning traces, allowing us to measure stepwise latent prediction formation. Our results reveal clear evidence of multilingual latent reasoning, though unevenly: strong in resource-rich languages, weaker in low-resource ones, and broadly less observable on harder benchmarks. To understand whether these differences reflect distinct internal mechanisms, we further perform representational analyses. Despite surface-level disparities, we find that the internal evolution of predictions is highly consistent across languages and broadly aligns with English -- a pattern suggesting an English-centered latent reasoning pathway.

papers.title: Language Lives in Sparse Dimensions: Toward Interpretable and Efficient Multilingual Control for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode language identity, and can we identify sparse, consistent dimensions that control the cross-lingual transition from shared representations to language-specific token spaces?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that cross-lingual transfer in LLMs is governed by a sparse, consistent set of language-specific dimensions in the residual stream, and introduces a training-free method to identify and manipulate these dimensions for controlled language switching.
papers.conclusion: Language-specific dimensions are a consistent and controllable mechanism underlying cross-lingual transfer in LLMs, enabling efficient and interpretable multilingual control through simple, training-free interventions.
papers.key_findings:
Language-specific dimensions are sparse and appear at consistent indices across intermediate to final layers of LLMs.
These dimensions can be identified with as few as 50 sentences of parallel or monolingual data.
Intervening on these dimensions by overwriting their values can switch the model's output language while preserving semantic content.
The proposed method outperforms prior neuron-based approaches (Neuron-Kojima and Neuron-Tang) on a multilingual generation control task.
There is significant overlap in language-specific dimensions across typologically similar languages (e.g., Chinese and Japanese share many dimensions).
papers.limitation:
Hyperparameters (e.g., anchor layer, scaling coefficient) were primarily tuned on Llama2-7B and transferred to other models (Llama3.1-8B, Aya23-8B), which may be suboptimal.
Evaluation is limited to multilingual generation control and question answering tasks; broader impact on downstream tasks (e.g., mathematics, summarization) and robustness across prompt formulations remains unexamined.
future_direction: Conduct systematic per-model hyperparameter search to optimize performance for each model individually.
Extend evaluation to a broader range of downstream tasks, incorporate task-specific metrics and human judgments, and assess robustness across different prompt formulations.
papers.abstract: Large language models exhibit strong multilingual capabilities despite limited exposure to non-English data. Prior studies show that English-centric large language models map multilingual content into English-aligned representations at intermediate layers and then project them back into target-language token spaces in the final layer. From this observation, we hypothesize that this cross-lingual transition is governed by a small and sparse set of dimensions, which occur at consistent indices across the intermediate to final layers. Building on this insight, we introduce a simple, training-free method to identify and manipulate these dimensions, requiring only as few as 50 sentences of either parallel or monolingual data. Experiments on a multilingual generation control task reveal the interpretability of these dimensions, demonstrating that the interventions in these dimensions can switch the output language while preserving semantic content, and that it surpasses the performance of prior neuron-based approaches at a substantially lower cost.

papers.title: Arithmetic Without Algorithms: Language Models Solve Math With a Bag of Heuristics
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) solve arithmetic reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms or by memorizing training data?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs solve arithmetic tasks by combining a sparse set of heuristic neurons, each implementing simple patterns, forming a 'bag of heuristics' rather than using a robust algorithm or memorization.
papers.conclusion: LLMs implement a bag of heuristics—a combination of many memorized rules—to perform arithmetic reasoning, rather than using robust algorithms or pure memorization.
papers.key_findings:
A sparse subset of MLP neurons in the arithmetic circuit implements simple heuristics for arithmetic.
Each heuristic neuron activates for specific input patterns and promotes corresponding answer tokens.
The combination of these heuristic neurons (a bag of heuristics) explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts.
This mechanism emerges early in training and persists as the main source of arithmetic accuracy.
The bag of heuristics fails to generalize perfectly, leading to errors when prompts lack sufficient associated heuristics or when heuristics have imperfect recall.
papers.limitation:
Human bias in defining heuristic types, as abstractions are based on human-identifiable definitions.
Analysis focuses on LLMs that tokenize multi-digit numbers as single tokens, which may not generalize to models with single-digit tokenization.
future_direction: Developing methods to identify heuristic abstractions without human bias.
Investigating if regularization can improve the bag of heuristics mechanism.
Exploring fundamental changes to training and architectures to improve mathematical abilities.
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) solve reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms, or do they memorize training data? To investigate this question, we use arithmetic reasoning as a representative task. Using causal analysis, we identify a subset of the model (a circuit) that explains most of the model's behavior for basic arithmetic logic and examine its functionality. By zooming in on the level of individual circuit neurons, we discover a sparse set of important neurons that implement simple heuristics. Each heuristic identifies a numerical input pattern and outputs corresponding answers. We hypothesize that the combination of these heuristic neurons is the mechanism used to produce correct arithmetic answers. To test this, we categorize each neuron into several heuristic types-such as neurons that activate when an operand falls within a certain range-and find that the unordered combination of these heuristic types is the mechanism that explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts. Finally, we demonstrate that this mechanism appears as the main source of arithmetic accuracy early in training. Overall, our experimental results across several LLMs show that LLMs perform arithmetic using neither robust algorithms nor memorization; rather, they rely on a "bag of heuristics".

papers.title: Reasoning Circuits in Language Models: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Syllogistic Inference
papers.research_question: How is content-independent syllogistic reasoning internalized in LMs during pre-training? Are content-independent mechanisms disentangled from world knowledge and belief biases? Does the core reasoning mechanism generalize across syllogistic schemes, model sizes, and architectures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a sufficient and necessary circuit for syllogistic reasoning involving middle-term suppression, showing that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms that are susceptible to contamination from world knowledge.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn transferable reasoning mechanisms but such mechanisms are contaminated and suppressed by the world knowledge acquired during pre-training, indicating a lack of generalizable abstract logical primitives.
papers.key_findings:
The circuit for syllogistic reasoning involves a three-stage mechanism: long induction, duplication, suppression, and mover heads.
The circuit is necessary and sufficient for symbolic syllogistic reasoning.
The circuit transfers to non-symbolic arguments but is contaminated by belief biases, with additional attention heads encoding world knowledge.
The circuit generalizes across unconditionally valid syllogistic schemes where models achieve high accuracy.
The suppression mechanism pattern is compatible across different model families and sizes, though with increasing complexity in larger models.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is confined to specific syllogistic reasoning templates and does not consider more complex scenarios.
The experimentation is confined due to the intricate level of granularity and computational complexity required in circuit analysis.
future_direction: Further studies to understand how the discovered symbolic circuit can be effectively disentangled from world knowledge to enable systematic generalization in LMs’ reasoning.
papers.abstract: Recent studies on reasoning in language models (LMs) have sparked a debate on whether they can learn systematic inferential principles or merely exploit superficial patterns in the training data. To understand and uncover the mechanisms adopted for formal reasoning in LMs, this paper presents a mechanistic interpretation of syllogistic inference. Specifically, we present a methodology for circuit discovery aimed at interpreting content-independent and formal reasoning mechanisms. Through two distinct intervention methods, we uncover a sufficient and necessary circuit involving middle-term suppression that elucidates how LMs transfer information to derive valid conclusions from premises. Furthermore, we investigate how belief biases manifest in syllogistic inference, finding evidence of partial contamination from additional attention heads responsible for encoding commonsense and contextualized knowledge. Finally, we explore the generalization of the discovered mechanisms across various syllogistic schemes, model sizes and architectures. The identified circuit is sufficient and necessary for syllogistic schemes on which the models achieve high accuracy (>60%), with compatible activation patterns across models of different families. Overall, our findings suggest that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms, but that, at the same time, such mechanisms do not involve generalizable and abstract logical primitives, being susceptible to contamination by the same world knowledge acquired during pre-training.

papers.title: Discovering Language-neutral Sub-networks in Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: To what extent do multilingual pre-trained language models learn language-neutral representations, and what is the effect of such representations on cross-lingual transfer performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that multilingual language models contain language-neutral sub-networks that are topologically similar across languages and can be effectively transferred for cross-lingual tasks, but this transferability decreases at higher sparsity levels.
papers.conclusion: The results suggest that multilingual language models include separate language-neutral and language-specific components, with the language-neutral components playing a more prominent role in cross-lingual transfer performance.
papers.key_findings:
Winning tickets (sub-networks) can be found for each language and task at multiple sparsity levels, though performance degrades at higher sparsity.
Sub-networks for different languages have high parameter overlap, especially for NER and XNLI tasks, indicating language-neutral components.
Cross-lingual transfer of winning tickets is effective for XNLI and NER, but less so for MLM, and transfer performance degrades at higher sparsity.
The language-neutral components are more prominent in the middle to upper layers of the model.
Combining multiple languages during pruning can yield sub-networks that transfer better to low-resource languages.
papers.limitation:
Parameter overlap may not be a fine-grained measure for identifying language-neutral components, as small differences in cross-lingual performance do not strongly correlate with overlap.
Only the lottery ticket hypothesis is used for discovering sub-networks, while other pruning and masking methods may provide complementary or competing insights.
Due to computational limitations, the analysis is limited to three tasks and eleven languages, and new insights may emerge from a larger cross-section.
papers.abstract: Multilingual pre-trained language models transfer remarkably well on cross-lingual downstream tasks. However, the extent to which they learn language-neutral representations (i.e., shared representations that encode similar phenomena across languages), and the effect of such representations on cross-lingual transfer performance, remain open questions. In this work, we conceptualize language neutrality of multilingual models as a function of the overlap between language-encoding subnetworks of these models. We employ the lottery ticket hypothesis to discover sub-networks that are individually optimized for various languages and tasks. Our evaluation across three distinct tasks and eleven typologically-diverse languages demonstrates that sub-networks for different languages are topologically similar (i.e., language-neutral), making them effective initializations for cross-lingual transfer with limited performance degradation. 1

papers.title: The Semantic Hub Hypothesis: Language Models Share Semantic Representations Across Languages and Modalities
papers.research_question: To what extent do language models learn and use a shared semantic representation space across different languages and modalities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the semantic hub hypothesis, which posits that language models learn a shared representation space across languages and modalities, and provides evidence through representation similarity and intervention experiments.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that language models learn a shared semantic representation space (the semantic hub) that is anchored by the dominant language and is causally involved in processing across languages and modalities.
papers.key_findings:
Model representations for semantically equivalent inputs in different languages are similar in intermediate layers.
The shared representation space is scaffolded by the model's dominant language (e.g., English) and can be interpreted via the logit lens.
This phenomenon extends to other data types: arithmetic expressions, code, images, and audio.
Interventions in the shared space using the dominant language affect model outputs in other data types, indicating causal usage.
The shared space is not just a byproduct but actively used during processing.
papers.limitation:
Chameleon-7B cannot answer more sophisticated reasoning questions about images, such as asking for a country flag or spatial relationships, even without interventions.
The logit lens analysis for audio is a lower bound because many words in labels (e.g., prepositions) are unlikely to be represented in the audio hidden states.
future_direction: Future work aimed at better controlling models using insights from the semantic hub hypothesis.
papers.abstract: Modern language models can process inputs across diverse languages and modalities. We hypothesize that models acquire this capability through learning a shared representation space across heterogeneous data types (e.g., different languages and modalities), which places semantically similar inputs near one another, even if they are from different modalities/languages. We term this the semantic hub hypothesis, following the hub-and-spoke model from neuroscience (Patterson et al., 2007) which posits that semantic knowledge in the human brain is organized through a transmodal semantic "hub" which integrates information from various modality-specific "spokes" regions. We first show that model representations for semantically equivalent inputs in different languages are similar in the intermediate layers, and that this space can be interpreted using the model's dominant pretraining language via the logit lens. This tendency extends to other data types, including arithmetic expressions, code, and visual/audio inputs. Interventions in the shared representation space in one data type also predictably affect model outputs in other data types, suggesting that this shared representations space is not simply a vestigial byproduct of large-scale training on broad data, but something that is actively utilized by the model during input processing.

papers.title: Linguistic Minimal Pairs Elicit Linguistic Similarity in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models represent different linguistic phenomena, and are linguistically similar phenomena represented similarly in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method using linguistic minimal pairs to measure linguistic similarity in LLMs, revealing that linguistic similarity is influenced by training data, aligns with fine-grained linguistic categories, weakly correlates with semantic similarity, and shows limited cross-lingual alignment.
papers.conclusion: The work provides insights into LLMs' internal language processing, bridging neural models and linguistic theory, and offers a foundation for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Linguistic similarity is significantly influenced by training data exposure, leading to higher cross-LLM agreement in higher-resource languages.
Linguistic similarity strongly aligns with fine-grained theoretical linguistic categories but weakly with broader ones.
Linguistic similarity shows a weak correlation with semantic similarity, indicating its context-dependent nature.
LLMs exhibit limited cross-lingual alignment in their understanding of relevant linguistic phenomena.
papers.limitation:
Dependent on the quality and scope of existing linguistic minimal pair datasets
Limited to three languages, not representing global linguistic diversity
Only captures a fraction of language's complexity with 150 phenomena
future_direction: Developing more high-quality minimal pairs
Broadening language coverage to include more diverse linguistic families
Increasing the range of phenomena studied
papers.abstract: We introduce a novel analysis that leverages linguistic minimal pairs to probe the internal linguistic representations of Large Language Models (LLMs). By measuring the similarity between LLM activation differences across minimal pairs, we quantify the and gain insight into the linguistic knowledge captured by LLMs. Our large-scale experiments, spanning 100+ LLMs and 150k minimal pairs in three languages, reveal properties of linguistic similarity from four key aspects: consistency across LLMs, relation to theoretical categorizations, dependency to semantic context, and cross-lingual alignment of relevant phenomena. Our findings suggest that 1) linguistic similarity is significantly influenced by training data exposure, leading to higher cross-LLM agreement in higher-resource languages. 2) Linguistic similarity strongly aligns with fine-grained theoretical linguistic categories but weakly with broader ones. 3) Linguistic similarity shows a weak correlation with semantic similarity, showing its context-dependent nature. 4) LLMs exhibit limited cross-lingual alignment in their understanding of relevant linguistic phenomena. This work demonstrates the potential of minimal pairs as a window into the neural representations of language in LLMs, shedding light on the relationship between LLMs and linguistic theory. Codes and data are available at https://github.com/ChenDelong1999/Linguistic-Similarity

papers.title: Are formal and functional linguistic mechanisms dissociated in language models?
papers.research_question: Do current large language models exhibit distinct localization (dissociation) of formal and functional linguistic mechanisms in their internal circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds evidence for formal-functional dissociation in LLMs in terms of cross-task faithfulness (formal task circuits perform other formal tasks better than functional ones, and vice-versa), but not in terms of circuit overlap, suggesting a shared pool of mechanisms for formal tasks rather than a single unified region.
papers.conclusion: There is evidence for emerging formal-functional dissociation in LLMs in terms of cross-task faithfulness, but not in terms of circuit overlap, indicating a set of shared formal linguistic mechanisms rather than a single unified region.
papers.key_findings:
Circuits for formal and functional linguistic tasks have low overlap (IoU).
Circuits for formal tasks do not have especially high overlap with each other, arguing against a single unified formal network.
Formal task circuits perform other formal tasks better than they perform functional tasks (cross-task faithfulness).
Functional task circuits perform other functional tasks better than they perform formal tasks (cross-task faithfulness).
Clustering based on cross-task faithfulness vectors separates formal and functional tasks into distinct groups.
papers.limitation: The circuit-finding method (EAP-IG) may not perfectly capture all relevant mechanisms, and the findings are limited to the specific models and tasks studied.
future_direction: Studying more models and tasks to generalize findings.
Using more granular analyses (e.g., neuron-level, sparse feature circuits).
Investigating the effects of model scale and architecture on dissociation.
papers.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) are increasingly capable, these capabilities are unevenly distributed: they excel at formal linguistic tasks, such as producing fluent, grammatical text, but struggle more with functional linguistic tasks like reasoning and consistent fact retrieval. Inspired by neuroscience, recent work suggests that to succeed on both formal and functional linguistic tasks, LLMs should use different mechanisms for each; such localization could either be built-in or emerge spontaneously through training. In this paper, we ask: do current models, with fast-improving functional linguistic abilities, exhibit distinct localization of formal and functional linguistic mechanisms? We answer this by finding and comparing the "circuits", or minimal computational subgraphs, responsible for various formal and functional tasks. Comparing 5 LLMs across 10 distinct tasks, we find that while there is indeed little overlap between circuits for formal and functional tasks, there is also little overlap between formal linguistic tasks, as exists in the human brain. Thus, a single formal linguistic network, unified and distinct from functional task circuits, remains elusive. However, in terms of cross-task faithfulness - the ability of one circuit to solve another's task - we observe a separation between formal and functional mechanisms, suggesting that shared mechanisms between formal tasks may exist.

papers.title: Do Llamas Work in English? On the Latent Language of Multilingual Transformers
papers.research_question: Do multilingual language models trained on unbalanced, English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language when processing non-English prompts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that multilingual language models like Llama-2 use English as an internal pivot language, with intermediate representations favoring English before shifting to the target language.
papers.conclusion: The evidence suggests that the abstract 'concept space' in multilingual transformers lies closer to English than to other languages, which may have important consequences regarding linguistic biases.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate embeddings in middle layers decode to English versions of the correct next token, even when the input and output are non-English.
The forward pass goes through three phases: input space (high entropy, no language), concept space (low entropy, English dominates), and output space (target language dominates).
The concept space is biased towards English, indicating an internal pivot language.
The English bias is less pronounced for languages with single-token words (like Chinese) in repetition tasks.
The token energy metric shows that latent embeddings have low energy in middle layers and high energy in later layers when the target language is selected.
papers.limitation:
Focus on the Llama-2 family limits generalizability to other models.
Tasks are simple and provide a highly controlled, toy-like context.
Limited understanding of the structure of the concept space in its original high-dimensional form.
The logit lens only grants approximate access to internal beliefs about output; other information remains hidden.
future_direction: Investigate how English bias changes when decreasing the dominance of English during training, e.g., by using different language mixtures or tokenizers.
Extend to a wider range of tasks, including more culturally sensitive problems and popular use-cases.
Better understand and map out the concept space in its high-dimensional form.
papers.abstract: We ask whether multilingual language models trained on unbalanced, English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language -- a question of key importance for understanding how language models function and the origins of linguistic bias. Focusing on the Llama-2 family of transformer models, our study uses carefully constructed non-English prompts with a unique correct single-token continuation. From layer to layer, transformers gradually map an input embedding of the final prompt token to an output embedding from which next-token probabilities are computed. Tracking intermediate embeddings through their high-dimensional space reveals three distinct phases, whereby intermediate embeddings (1) start far away from output token embeddings; (2) already allow for decoding a semantically correct next token in the middle layers, but give higher probability to its version in English than in the input language; (3) finally move into an input-language-specific region of the embedding space. We cast these results into a conceptual model where the three phases operate in "input space", "concept space", and "output space", respectively. Crucially, our evidence suggests that the abstract "concept space" lies closer to English than to other languages, which may have important consequences regarding the biases held by multilingual language models.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others
papers.research_question: Do large language models develop internal representations of self and others' beliefs, and what is the functional role of these representations in social reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that large language models develop linearly decodable internal representations of self and others' beliefs in their attention heads, and that manipulating these representations causally alters the model's theory-of-mind performance.
papers.conclusion: Language models develop internal representations of self and others' beliefs that are linearly decodable and play a causal role in social reasoning, suggesting a mechanistic basis for their theory-of-mind capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can decode the belief status (true/false) of both the protagonist and an omniscient oracle from the activations of specific attention heads in language models.
A subset of attention heads, primarily in middle layers, encodes the belief statuses of both agents independently and in conjunction.
Steering activations along directions that amplify the protagonist's belief and distinguish it from the oracle's belief (+TpFo) significantly improves model performance on false-belief tasks.
The identified belief representations are general and correlated across different social reasoning tasks (Forward Belief, Forward Action, Backward Belief).
Activation interventions along random or single-agent belief directions have minimal impact, highlighting the specificity of the multi-agent belief representation.
papers.abstract: Understanding and attributing mental states, known as Theory of Mind (ToM), emerges as a fundamental capability for human social reasoning. While Large Language Models (LLMs) appear to possess certain ToM abilities, the mechanisms underlying these capabilities remain elusive. In this study, we discover that it is possible to linearly decode the belief status from the perspectives of various agents through neural activations of language models, indicating the existence of internal representations of self and others' beliefs. By manipulating these representations, we observe dramatic changes in the models' ToM performance, underscoring their pivotal role in the social reasoning process. Additionally, our findings extend to diverse social reasoning tasks that involve different causal inference patterns, suggesting the potential generalizability of these representations.

papers.title: Exploring the Translation Mechanism of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the crucial components and their behavioral patterns in LLM translation, and can fine-tuning these components enhance translation capability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework using subspace-intervened path patching to identify sparse, specialized components crucial for LLM translation, and shows that fine-tuning these components improves translation while preserving general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: The translation mechanism in LLMs is driven by a sparse set of specialized components, and targeted intervention on these components can enhance translation performance without harming general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Only a sparse subset of heads (less than 5%) are crucial for LLMs’ translation.
Crucial heads exhibit specialized functions (source, indicator, positional) and MLPs integrate their features into English-centric latent representations.
Fine-tuning merely 64 heads achieves performance parity with full-parameter fine-tuning.
These crucial components generalize to sentence-level translation and other tasks (mathematical reasoning).
The translation mechanism is largely established during pre-training, not fine-tuning.
papers.limitation: The analysis is primarily conducted on word-level translation, which may not fully capture the complexities of sentence-level translation.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) demonstrate remarkable success in multilingual translation, their internal core translation mechanisms, even at the fundamental word level, remain insufficiently understood. To address this critical gap, this work introduces a systematic framework for interpreting the mechanism behind LLM translation from the perspective of computational components. This paper first proposes subspace-intervened path patching for precise, fine-grained causal analysis, enabling the detection of components crucial to translation tasks and subsequently characterizing their behavioral patterns in human-interpretable terms. Comprehensive experiments reveal that translation is predominantly driven by a sparse subset of components: specialized attention heads serve critical roles in extracting source language, translation indicators, and positional features, which are then integrated and processed by specific multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) into intermediary English-centric latent representations before ultimately yielding the final translation. The significance of these findings is underscored by the empirical demonstration that targeted fine-tuning a minimal parameter subset ($<5\%$) enhances translation performance while preserving general capabilities. This result further indicates that these crucial components generalize effectively to sentence-level translation and are instrumental in elucidating more intricate translation tasks.

papers.title: When Meanings Meet: Investigating the Emergence and Quality of Shared Concept Spaces during Multilingual Language Model Training
papers.research_question: How do shared, language-agnostic concept spaces emerge and develop during the multilingual pretraining of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Shared concept spaces emerge early in multilingual pretraining and remain relatively stable, but alignment with these spaces is language-dependent and influenced by training data composition.
papers.conclusion: Shared concept spaces emerge early and are progressively refined during multilingual pretraining, with alignment depending on language and data composition. Targeted multi-aligned data can improve alignment for low-resource languages.
papers.key_findings:
Shared concept spaces arise early in pretraining and continue to refine throughout training.
Alignment with shared concept spaces depends on language similarity and training data proportion.
Cross-lingual concept patching can shift model behavior, such as selecting dominant senses for polysemous words or translating cross-lingual homographs instead of copying them.
The model initially prefers copying input words over translating them, a behavior learned early.
Patching from averaged representations across languages (the 'seen' setting) is often as effective as patching from English-only representations for inducing concepts in English output.
papers.limitation:
Focuses primarily on a single, relatively small model (EuroLLM-1.7B), though provides supporting evidence on two others.
Analysis is restricted to nouns; behavior of other word classes is not studied.
Inherits biases from the Multi-SimLex dataset, such as ambiguous translations for polysemous words.
Focuses only on the simple task of word-level translation; findings may not generalize to more complex tasks.
future_direction: Investigate how representations for other word classes (beyond nouns) behave.
Study the emergence and behavior of language-agnostic spaces for more complex multilingual tasks like sentence-level translation or reasoning.
papers.abstract: Training Large Language Models (LLMs) with high multilingual coverage is becoming increasingly important -- especially when monolingual resources are scarce. Recent studies have found that LLMs process multilingual inputs in shared concept spaces, thought to support generalization and cross-lingual transfer. However, these prior studies often do not use causal methods, lack deeper error analysis or focus on the final model only, leaving open how these spaces emerge during training. We investigate the development of language-agnostic concept spaces during pretraining of EuroLLM through the causal interpretability method of activation patching. We isolate cross-lingual concept representations, then inject them into a translation prompt to investigate how consistently translations can be altered, independently of the language. We find that shared concept spaces emerge early} and continue to refine, but that alignment with them is language-dependent}. Furthermore, in contrast to prior work, our fine-grained manual analysis reveals that some apparent gains in translation quality reflect shifts in behavior -- like selecting senses for polysemous words or translating instead of copying cross-lingual homographs -- rather than improved translation ability. Our findings offer new insight into the training dynamics of cross-lingual alignment and the conditions under which causal interpretability methods offer meaningful insights in multilingual contexts.

papers.title: Cross-Lingual Activation Steering for Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: How can inference-time neuron activation steering improve cross-lingual transfer in multilingual language models without additional training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Cross-Lingual Activation Steering (CLAS), a training-free inference-time method that modulates neuron activations to improve cross-lingual transfer in multilingual LLMs by rebalancing shared and language-specific representations.
papers.conclusion: CLAS effectively improves cross-lingual transfer in multilingual LLMs by steering activations to promote functional divergence, with gains not reliant on geometric alignment to the anchor language.
papers.key_findings:
CLAS achieves average improvements of 2.3% (Acc.) and 3.4% (F1) on classification and generation benchmarks, respectively.
Performance improvements are driven by functional divergence, with gains correlating with increased language cluster separation rather than closer alignment to English.
CLAS reduces cosine similarity to English for non-anchor languages, indicating a shift away from strict geometric alignment.
Qualitative analysis shows CLAS suppresses repetition loops and verbosity in generation outputs.
The steering parameter alpha can be positive or negative for optimal performance, indicating task- and model-dependent balance between shared and language-specific signals.
papers.limitation:
Analysis and intervention are anchored to English, which may not generalize to other anchor languages.
CLAS is not uniformly beneficial and can cause performance regressions for some languages.
Mechanistic analysis does not isolate attention heads or other circuit components, limiting causal attribution.
future_direction: Explore adaptive steering strategies based on representational structure.
Better understand saturation effects in well-separated language clusters.
Extend CLAS to other modalities and training settings.
papers.abstract: Large language models exhibit strong multilingual capabilities, yet significant performance gaps persist between dominant and non-dominant languages. Prior work attributes this gap to imbalances between shared and language-specific neurons in multilingual representations. We propose Cross-Lingual Activation Steering (CLAS), a training-free inference-time intervention that selectively modulates neuron activations. We evaluate CLAS on classification and generation benchmarks, achieving average improvements of 2.3% (Acc.) and 3.4% (F1) respectively, while maintaining high-resource language performance. We discover that effective transfer operates through functional divergence rather than strict alignment; performance gains correlate with increased language cluster separation. Our results demonstrate that targeted activation steering can unlock latent multilingual capacity in existing models without modification to model weights.

papers.title: Semantic Pivots Enable Cross-Lingual Transfer in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to quantify, understand, and improve the cross-lingual ability of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a word-level cross-lingual translation task and dataset (CLWTD) to quantify cross-lingual ability, identifies co-occurrence and semantic pivot behaviors in LLMs, links them to dataset co-occurrence, and shows that constructing a semantic pivot-aware pre-training dataset improves cross-lingual ability.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a word-level task to quantify cross-lingual ability, identifies and distinguishes two behaviors, attributes them to co-occurrence frequency, finds semantic pivots from the dataset, and improves cross-lingual ability by reconstructing a pre-training dataset.
papers.key_findings:
The Cross-Lingual Word Translation Dataset (CLWTD) provides a continuous metric that accurately reflects LLMs' cross-lingual ability.
LLMs exhibit two distinct behaviors during word translation: co-occurrence behavior and semantic pivot behavior.
These behaviors are attributed to the co-occurrence frequency of words in the pre-training dataset.
Semantic pivots can be identified from the pre-training data and show a probability trend in intermediate layers.
Constructing a pre-training dataset with a high proportion of semantic pivots effectively enhances cross-lingual ability.
papers.limitation: Due to limited availability of open-source large language models with public checkpoints and pre-training data, experiments are only validated on the OLMo-1B model.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate remarkable ability in cross-lingual tasks. Understanding how LLMs acquire this ability is crucial for their interpretability. To quantify the cross-lingual ability of LLMs accurately, we propose a Word-Level Cross-Lingual Translation Task. To find how LLMs learn cross-lingual ability, we trace the outputs of LLMs' intermediate layers in the word translation task. We identify and distinguish two distinct behaviors in the forward pass of LLMs: co-occurrence behavior and semantic pivot behavior. We attribute LLMs' two distinct behaviors to the co-occurrence frequency of words and find the semantic pivot from the pre-training dataset.
