Finally, we also discuss the implication of cognitive modeling of these results.

papers.title: Tracing the Roots of Facts in Multilingual Language Models: Independent, Shared, and Transferred Knowledge
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how factual knowledge is acquired and represented in multilingual language models, examining performance differences across languages, shared vs. independent representations, and mechanisms of cross-lingual transfer.
papers.core_contribution: This paper identifies three patterns of fact representation in multilingual language models—language-independent, cross-lingual shared, and cross-lingual transferred—and reveals limited effectiveness of cross-lingual knowledge transfer.
papers.conclusion: The study highlights the challenges in achieving effective cross-lingual transfer of factual knowledge and underscores the need for better representation learning and probing datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Factual probing performance varies across languages with moderate correlation to training data volume.
ML-LMs exhibit both language-independent and cross-lingual fact representations based on neuron activity patterns.
Cross-lingual knowledge transfer is limited and often localized to geographically proximate languages.
Easy-to-predict facts include shared entity tokens and naming cues, reducing apparent cross-lingual transfer.
Active neurons for facts in low-resource languages are more distributed in shallow layers compared to high-resource languages.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to encoder-based models (mBERT and XLM-R), and findings may not generalize to decoder-based models like BLOOM.
future_direction: Enhance cross-lingual fact representation learning in ML-LMs.
Develop a more precise factual probing dataset.
papers.abstract: Acquiring factual knowledge for language models (LMs) in low-resource languages poses a serious challenge, thus resorting to cross-lingual transfer in multilingual LMs (ML-LMs). In this study, we ask how ML-LMs acquire and represent factual knowledge. Using the multilingual factual knowledge probing dataset, mLAMA, we first conducted a neuron investigation of ML-LMs (specifically, multilingual BERT). We then traced the roots of facts back to the knowledge source (Wikipedia) to identify the ways in which ML-LMs acquire specific facts. We finally identified three patterns of acquiring and representing facts in ML-LMs: language-independent, cross-lingual shared and transferred, and devised methods for differentiating them. Our findings highlight the challenge of maintaining consistent factual knowledge across languages, underscoring the need for better fact representation learning in ML-LMs.

papers.title: Steering into New Embedding Spaces: Analyzing Cross-Lingual Alignment Induced by Model Interventions in Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the effect of the finding experts intervention on cross-lingual alignment in multilingual language models?
papers.core_contribution: Intervening on language expert neurons in mLLMs projects embeddings into a new space with enhanced cross-lingual alignment, leading to improved performance on cross-lingual retrieval tasks.
papers.conclusion: The finding-experts intervention enhances cross-lingual alignment in mLLMs, improving retrieval performance, and is recommended for aligning representations across languages.
papers.key_findings:
The finding experts intervention shifts the embedding space, reducing distances between languages and increasing cross-lingual alignment.
Post-intervention, cross-lingual retrieval accuracy improves by up to 2x in top-1 accuracy.
Within-language similarity is preserved in the new embedding space, as shown by paraphrase retrieval accuracy.
Intervention on random neurons does not yield similar improvements, indicating the importance of targeting expert neurons.
The intervention is most effective when the model has been trained on both the intervention-target and the languages to be aligned.
papers.limitation:
Lack of access to training data and procedures for the models, limiting deeper analysis.
PolyLM-13b behaves as an outlier in the analyses, possibly due to training differences.
Only one intervention method (finding experts) is studied, leaving other approaches for future work.
future_direction: Explore the effect of intervention on alignment in controlled settings with known training data.
Compare different model intervention methods to understand their impact on representation space.
papers.abstract: Aligned representations across languages is a desired property in multilingual large language models (mLLMs), as alignment can improve performance in cross-lingual tasks. Typically alignment requires fine-tuning a model, which is computationally expensive, and sizable language data, which often may not be available. A data-efficient alternative to fine-tuning is model interventions -- a method for manipulating model activations to steer generation into the desired direction. We analyze the effect of a popular intervention (finding experts) on the alignment of cross-lingual representations in mLLMs. We identify the neurons to manipulate for a given language and introspect the embedding space of mLLMs pre- and post-manipulation. We show that modifying the mLLM's activations changes its embedding space such that cross-lingual alignment is enhanced. Further, we show that the changes to the embedding space translate into improved downstream performance on retrieval tasks, with up to 2x improvements in top-1 accuracy on cross-lingual retrieval.

papers.title: On the Linguistic Representational Power of Neural Machine Translation Models
papers.research_question: How do neural machine translation models capture linguistic information (morphology, syntax, semantics) in their representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that neural machine translation models learn non-trivial linguistic information in their representations, with a hierarchical organization: lower layers capture local, low-level properties (morphology) and higher layers capture global, high-level properties (syntax, semantics).
papers.conclusion: Deep NMT models trained in an end-to-end fashion, without direct supervision, learn a substantial amount of linguistic information, and the representations are organized in a hierarchical manner.
papers.key_findings:
Word morphology and part-of-speech information are captured at the lower layers of the model.
Lexical semantics and non-local syntactic and semantic dependencies are better represented at the higher layers of the model.
Representations learned using characters are more informed about word-morphology compared to those learned using subword units.
Representations learned by multilingual models are richer compared to bilingual models.
The target language impacts the kind of information learned by the MT system, with translation into morphologically-poorer languages leading to better source-side word representations.
papers.abstract: Despite the recent success of deep neural networks in natural language processing and other spheres of artificial intelligence, their interpretability remains a challenge. We analyze the representations learned by neural machine translation (NMT) models at various levels of granularity and evaluate their quality through relevant extrinsic properties. In particular, we seek answers to the following questions: (i) How accurately is word structure captured within the learned representations, which is an important aspect in translating morphologically rich languages? (ii) Do the representations capture long-range dependencies, and effectively handle syntactically divergent languages? (iii) Do the representations capture lexical semantics? We conduct a thorough investigation along several parameters: (i) Which layers in the architecture capture each of these linguistic phenomena; (ii) How does the choice of translation unit (word, character, or subword unit) impact the linguistic properties captured by the underlying representations? (iii) Do the encoder and decoder learn differently and independently? (iv) Do the representations learned by multilingual NMT models capture the same amount of linguistic information as their bilingual counterparts? Our data-driven, quantitative evaluation illuminates important aspects in NMT models and their ability to capture various linguistic phenomena. We show that deep NMT models trained in an end-to-end fashion, without being provided any direct supervision during the training process, learn a non-trivial amount of linguistic information. Notable findings include the following observations: (i) Word morphology and part-of-speech information are captured at the lower layers of the model; (ii) In contrast, lexical semantics or non-local syntactic and semantic dependencies are better represented at the higher layers of the model; (iii) Representations learned using characters are more informed about word-morphology compared to those learned using subword units; and (iv) Representations learned by multilingual models are richer compared to bilingual models.

papers.title: Can LLMs Lie? Investigation beyond Hallucination
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether LLMs can intentionally lie (as opposed to unintentionally hallucinate), and how to understand and control lying behavior using mechanistic interpretability.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers the neural mechanisms of lying in LLMs using mechanistic interpretability, and introduces steering vectors to control lying behavior, showing a trade-off between honesty and task performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that lying in LLMs can be understood and controlled via mechanistic interpretability, and highlights the trade-offs between honesty and task success in real-world scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
Lying ability in LLMs improves with model size and reasoning capabilities.
LLMs use dummy tokens as a computational scratchpad for lying, with specific attention heads and MLP modules involved.
Lying circuits are sparse and can be ablated to reduce deception without broadly degrading model utility.
Different types of lies (white vs. malicious, commission vs. omission) are linearly separable in activation space and controllable via distinct steering directions.
Steering vectors can increase honesty in multi-turn conversational settings, establishing a Pareto frontier between honesty and goal completion.
papers.limitation:
Analysis confined to a few model families and sizes.
Steering vectors derived from a limited set of contrastive prompts.
Multi-turn conversational setting is simplified.
Honesty steering vectors applied in the negative direction may lead to mass production of false information.
future_direction: Scaling the approach to larger models and more complex scenarios.
Investigating the transferability of steering vectors across domains.
Developing more robust safeguards against deceptive AI.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across a variety of tasks, but their increasing autonomy in real-world applications raises concerns about their trustworthiness. While hallucinations-unintentional falsehoods-have been widely studied, the phenomenon of lying, where an LLM knowingly generates falsehoods to achieve an ulterior objective, remains underexplored. In this work, we systematically investigate the lying behavior of LLMs, differentiating it from hallucinations and testing it in practical scenarios. Through mechanistic interpretability techniques, we uncover the neural mechanisms underlying deception, employing logit lens analysis, causal interventions, and contrastive activation steering to identify and control deceptive behavior. We study real-world lying scenarios and introduce behavioral steering vectors that enable fine-grained manipulation of lying tendencies. Further, we explore the trade-offs between lying and end-task performance, establishing a Pareto frontier where dishonesty can enhance goal optimization. Our findings contribute to the broader discourse on AI ethics, shedding light on the risks and potential safeguards for deploying LLMs in high-stakes environments. Code and more illustrations are available at https://llm-liar.github.io/

papers.title: Paths Not Taken: Understanding and Mending the Multilingual Factual Recall Pipeline
papers.research_question: Why do multilingual large language models exhibit factual inconsistencies across languages, and how can these failures be understood and mended?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a multilingual factual recall pipeline where LLMs use an English-centric mechanism and then translate answers, and introduces two vector interventions to fix errors in translation and recall, significantly improving cross-lingual factual consistency.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic insights into the multilingual processing pipeline can be used to design targeted, training-free interventions that direct the model toward better internal paths, unlocking latent multilingual capabilities and improving factual consistency.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual LLMs employ a pipeline where factual information is first retrieved in English using intermediate English-centric mechanisms, followed by translation into the target language in later layers.
Two primary failure points cause cross-lingual inconsistencies: insufficient engagement of the reliable English-centric recall mechanism, and incorrect translation from English back to the target language.
A translation difference vector intervention, derived from the activation difference between explicit translation and fact-recall tasks, steers the model to use more effective translation components, improving conversion correctness.
A recall task vector intervention, extracted from in-context learning examples, promotes the engagement of English-centric factual recall components (like relation propagation and answer extraction) for multilingual prompts.
Combining both interventions leads to substantial improvements in factual recall accuracy, boosting performance by up to 37.6 percentage points for the lowest-performing language and an average gain of 19.04 points across all evaluated languages.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to five non-English languages and ten relations on a single model (Llama-3.2-3B).
future_direction: Expanding the investigation to more diverse language families and syntactic structures.
Quantifying how the findings apply to relations of varying complexity or different models.
Developing automated methods to identify such weaknesses and implement corresponding solutions.
papers.abstract: Multilingual large language models (LLMs) often exhibit factual inconsistencies across languages, with significantly better performance in factual recall tasks in English than in other languages. The causes of these failures, however, remain poorly understood. Using mechanistic analysis techniques, we uncover the underlying pipeline that LLMs employ, which involves using the English-centric factual recall mechanism to process multilingual queries and then translating English answers back into the target language. We identify two primary sources of error: insufficient engagement of the reliable English-centric mechanism for factual recall, and incorrect translation from English back into the target language for the final answer. To address these vulnerabilities, we introduce two vector interventions, both independent of languages and datasets, to redirect the model toward better internal paths for higher factual consistency. Our interventions combined increase the recall accuracy by over 35 percent for the lowest-performing language. Our findings demonstrate how mechanistic insights can be used to unlock latent multilingual capabilities in LLMs.

papers.title: How Programming Concepts and Neurons Are Shared in Code Language Models
papers.research_question: How do code language models represent multiple programming languages and English in their concept space? Specifically, do they use a pivot language, and can we identify language-specific neurons?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates how code language models represent programming languages and English, finding that English and certain PLs (like C#) are central in the concept space, and that language-specific neurons exist but are challenging to identify for highly aligned PLs.
papers.conclusion: Our findings deepen our understanding of LLMs’ inner workings in the context of PLs and provide valuable insights for interpretability in code-related tasks.
papers.key_findings:
English and PL keywords appear in intermediate layers with high probabilities in the second half of the layers.
C# is highly aligned with other PLs in the model's concept space.
Language-specific neurons are concentrated in bottom layers, while PL-exclusive neurons are in top layers.
For highly aligned PLs (like C# and Java), identifying language-specific neurons is challenging.
The model's concept space is closer to English and assigns high probabilities to English tokens in intermediate layers during translation tasks.
papers.limitation:
The super-parallel dataset is limited to seven languages due to source constraints.
Using keywords to interpret latent embeddings may not be precise because some PL keywords lack direct English meanings or map to multiple tokens.
The analysis is limited to Llama-based architectures; exploring other architectures is needed for broader validation.
papers.abstract: Several studies have explored the mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) in coding tasks, but most have focused on programming languages (PLs) in a monolingual setting. In this paper, we investigate the relationship between multiple PLs and English in the concept space of LLMs. We perform a few-shot translation task on 21 PL pairs using two Llama-based models. By decoding the embeddings of intermediate layers during this task, we observe that the concept space is closer to English (including PL keywords) and assigns high probabilities to English tokens in the second half of the intermediate layers. We analyze neuron activations for 11 PLs and English, finding that while language-specific neurons are primarily concentrated in the bottom layers, those exclusive to each PL tend to appear in the top layers. For PLs that are highly aligned with multiple other PLs, identifying language-specific neurons is not feasible. These PLs also tend to have a larger keyword set than other PLs and are closer to the model's concept space regardless of the input/output PL in the translation task. Our findings provide insights into how LLMs internally represent PLs, revealing structural patterns in the model's concept space. Code is available at https://github.com/cisnlp/code-specific-neurons.

papers.title: Language Models as Artificial Learners: Investigating Crosslinguistic Influence
papers.research_question: How do L1 dominance and L2 proficiency affect crosslinguistic influence in language models, and can LMs serve as a computational framework to study human CLI?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that language models can simulate crosslinguistic influence, showing that L1 dominance and L2 proficiency predict CLI, and provides mechanistic evidence of L1 co-activation during L2 processing.
papers.conclusion: LMs can serve as artificial learners to study CLI, and the findings suggest a hybrid account where shared structures are bidirectionally primed, while non-overlapping structures are separate-but-connected and influenced by dominance.
papers.key_findings:
CLI effects are modulated by syntactic distance: similar L1 languages cause less interference or more facilitation.
Crosslinguistic priming is bidirectional for grammatical structures but sensitive to language dominance for ungrammatical structures.
LMs show preference for non-native constructions from the same L1, especially after priming.
LogitLens shows L1 token presence during L2 processing increases with L1 dominance.
L2 neuron overlap between L1 languages correlates negatively with syntactic distance.
papers.abstract: Despite the centrality of crosslinguistic influence (CLI) to bilingualism research, human studies often yield conflicting results due to inherent experimental variance. We address these inconsistencies by using language models (LMs) as controlled statistical learners to systematically simulate CLI and isolate its underlying drivers. Specifically, we study the effect of varying the L1 language dominance and the L2 language proficiency, which we manipulate by controlling the L2 age of exposure -- defined as the training step at which the L2 is introduced. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of pretraining on L1 languages with varying syntactic distance from the L2. Using cross-linguistic priming, we analyze how activating L1 structures impacts L2 processing. Our results align with evidence from psycholinguistic studies, confirming that language dominance and proficiency are strong predictors of CLI. We further find that while priming of grammatical structures is bidirectional, the priming of ungrammatical structures is sensitive to language dominance. Finally, we provide mechanistic evidence of CLI in LMs, demonstrating that the L1 is co-activated during L2 processing and directly influences the neural circuitry recruited for the L2. More broadly, our work demonstrates that LMs can serve as a computational framework to inform theories of human CLI.

papers.title: A Reply to Makelov et al. (2023)'s "Interpretability Illusion" Arguments
papers.research_question: Are the phenomena identified by Makelov et al. (2023) as 'interpretability illusions' actually inherent properties of distributed representations in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that the 'interpretability illusions' identified by Makelov et al. (2023) are not illusions but inherent properties of distributed representations, and provides additional experiments using DAS to analyze causal mechanisms in GPT-2.
papers.conclusion: The phenomena labeled as 'interpretability illusions' are inherent to distributed representations, and the work by Makelov et al. (2023) has advanced the field of mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Even directions considered non-illusory by Makelov et al. can be classified as illusory under their own definition.
The illusions reported by Makelov et al. are artifacts of their training and evaluation paradigms.
DAS can reproduce and extend findings on the IOI task, showing that name position information in GPT-2 is distributed across attention heads and emerges in the 8th layer.
Name position information is not carried by MLP activations but by the self-attention block in the 8th layer.
The correct IO name representation is distributed across multiple attention heads in the 9th layer.
papers.abstract: We respond to the recent paper by Makelov et al. (2023), which reviews subspace interchange intervention methods like distributed alignment search (DAS; Geiger et al. 2023) and claims that these methods potentially cause "interpretability illusions". We first review Makelov et al. (2023)'s technical notion of what an "interpretability illusion" is, and then we show that even intuitive and desirable explanations can qualify as illusions in this sense. As a result, their method of discovering "illusions" can reject explanations they consider "non-illusory". We then argue that the illusions Makelov et al. (2023) see in practice are artifacts of their training and evaluation paradigms. We close by emphasizing that, though we disagree with their core characterization, Makelov et al. (2023)'s examples and discussion have undoubtedly pushed the field of interpretability forward.

papers.title: Interpretability in the Wild: a Circuit for Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 small
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 small perform the indirect object identification (IOI) task, and what internal circuit is responsible for this behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and validates a circuit of 26 attention heads in GPT-2 small that performs indirect object identification, using a combination of interpretability techniques and quantitative criteria for faithfulness, completeness, and minimality.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, providing a step towards scaling interpretability to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Discovered a circuit of 26 attention heads grouped into 7 classes (e.g., Name Mover Heads, S-Inhibition Heads) that implement the IOI task.
Identified redundant behavior such as Backup Name Mover Heads that activate when regular Name Mover Heads are ablated.
Found that Negative Name Mover Heads write in the opposite direction, potentially to hedge predictions.
Formulated and evaluated quantitative criteria (faithfulness, completeness, minimality) to validate circuit explanations.
The circuit shows significant but incomplete understanding, with gaps in completeness and minimality.
papers.limitation:
Not fully understanding some components, such as the attention patterns of S-Inhibition Heads and the role of MLPs and layer norms.
The circuit is not completely complete or minimal, as shown by quantitative criteria.
The analysis is limited to GPT-2 small, which is much smaller than state-of-the-art models.
future_direction: Scale the approach to larger models like GPT-2 medium.
Investigate the behavior of the circuit on adversarial examples.
Understand the compensation effect in Backup Name Mover Heads.
papers.abstract: Research in mechanistic interpretability seeks to explain behaviors of machine learning models in terms of their internal components. However, most previous work either focuses on simple behaviors in small models, or describes complicated behaviors in larger models with broad strokes. In this work, we bridge this gap by presenting an explanation for how GPT-2 small performs a natural language task called indirect object identification (IOI). Our explanation encompasses 26 attention heads grouped into 7 main classes, which we discovered using a combination of interpretability approaches relying on causal interventions. To our knowledge, this investigation is the largest end-to-end attempt at reverse-engineering a natural behavior "in the wild" in a language model. We evaluate the reliability of our explanation using three quantitative criteria--faithfulness, completeness and minimality. Though these criteria support our explanation, they also point to remaining gaps in our understanding. Our work provides evidence that a mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, opening opportunities to scale our understanding to both larger models and more complex tasks.

papers.title: RomanLens: The Role Of Latent Romanization In Multilinguality In LLMs
papers.research_question: How do LLMs achieve multilingual capabilities, and specifically, what is the role of Romanization in multilingual processing for non-Roman script languages?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs use latent romanization as a bridge for processing non-Roman script languages, with romanized representations appearing in intermediate layers and target words emerging earlier when translated into romanized script.
papers.conclusion: LLMs implicitly use Romanization as a bridge for non-Roman scripts, with latent romanization occurring in intermediate layers and Romanization serving as a structural link between language-agnostic concepts and language-specific output.
papers.key_findings:
Latent Romanization occurs in intermediate layers during multilingual next-token generation, with romanized tokens appearing before native script.
Semantic concepts are encoded similarly regardless of whether the input is in native or Romanized script.
Romanized target representations emerge 1-2 layers earlier than native script representations in translation tasks.
Latent romanization is observed across multiple non-Roman script languages (except Chinese).
The repetition task shows a higher frequency of latent romanization compared to translation and cloze tasks.
papers.limitation:
The specific mechanisms by which LLMs adjust their interactions over different timesteps during token generation are not fully understood.
Interpretability of non-Roman scripts at latent layers is limited when models use tokenization schemes that split characters into multiple bytes.
The selective occurrence and varying intensity of latent romanization across languages are not explained.
future_direction: Develop training strategies that enhance performance across diverse linguistic communities.
Extend the work to models with alternative tokenization methods for a more complete understanding.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong multilingual performance despite being predominantly trained on English-centric corpora. This raises a fundamental question: How do LLMs achieve such multilingual capabilities? Focusing on languages written in non-Roman scripts, we investigate the role of Romanization—the representation of non-Roman scripts using Roman characters—as a potential bridge in multilingual processing. Using mechanistic interpretability techniques, we analyze next-token generation and find that intermediate layers frequently represent target words in Romanized form before transitioning to native script, a phenomenon we term Latent Romanization. Further, through activation patching experiments, we demonstrate that LLMs encode semantic concepts similarly across native and Romanized scripts, suggesting a shared underlying representation. Additionally, for translation into non-Roman script languages, our findings reveal that when the target language is in Romanized form, its representations emerge earlier in the model’s layers compared to native script. These insights contribute to a deeper understanding of multilingual representation in LLMs and highlight the implicit role of Romanization in facilitating language transfer.

papers.title: Computational Basis of LLM's Decision Making in Social Simulation
papers.research_question: How are social meanings internally represented in LLMs, and how can those internal representations be systematically manipulated to steer model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework for extracting and manipulating social concept vectors in LLMs' residual streams to steer decision-making in social simulations, specifically demonstrated in a Dictator Game.
papers.conclusion: The method provides a practical bridge between sociological theory and the internal geometry of modern language models, turning LLMs from opaque black boxes into calibrated instruments for theory testing, bounded synthetic data, and auditable interventions.
papers.key_findings:
Social variables like framing (give vs. take) and social distance (stranger meet) significantly affect the LLM's decision to transfer money in the Dictator Game.
These variables are encoded as vectors in the residual stream, and their alignment with the decision vector can be measured via cosine similarity and dot product.
By projecting and injecting these variable vectors into the residual stream, the model's decisions can be steered in a controlled manner.
The steering effect is layer-dependent and can be fine-tuned by adjusting the injection coefficient, with earlier layers having more amplified effects.
The method allows for precise manipulation of specific variables (e.g., gender) without affecting others, enabling targeted interventions.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on internal representational validity and controlled steering within the model's activation space, but does not establish external sociological validity (i.e., correspondence to human cognition and behavior).
The method requires access to the model's internal weights and activations, so it is only feasible with open-weight models.
future_direction: From Scripts to User-Friendly Tools: developing a user-friendly software package to make activation-based steering more accessible.
Expanding to other Social Constructs and Experiments: applying the framework to a wider range of social constructs and experimental paradigms.
Bridging the Gap Between Internal and External Validity: conducting systematic human-LLM comparisons to establish external sociological validity.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly serve as human-like decision-making agents in social science and applied settings. These LLM-agents are typically assigned human-like characters and placed in real-life contexts. However, how these characters and contexts shape an LLM's behavior remains underexplored. This study proposes and tests methods for probing, quantifying, and modifying an LLM's internal representations in a Dictator Game, a classic behavioral experiment on fairness and prosocial behavior. We extract ``vectors of variable variations'' (e.g., ``male'' to ``female'') from the LLM's internal state. Manipulating these vectors during the model's inference can substantially alter how those variables relate to the model's decision-making. This approach offers a principled way to study and regulate how social concepts can be encoded and engineered within transformer-based models, with implications for alignment, debiasing, and designing AI agents for social simulations in both academic and commercial applications, strengthening sociological theory and measurement.

papers.title: Disentangling Language and Culture for Evaluating Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how to evaluate multilingual large language models by disentangling linguistic medium and cultural context, and explores the Cultural-Linguistic Synergy phenomenon where models perform better when questions are culturally aligned with the language.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a Dual Evaluation Framework that disentangles language and culture to evaluate multilingual LLMs, and discovers the Cultural-Linguistic Synergy phenomenon where models perform better when questions are culturally aligned with the language.
papers.conclusion: The findings reveal the Cultural-Linguistic Synergy phenomenon, challenging the assumption that LLMs perform uniformly across languages, and highlight the necessity of culturally and linguistically aware model evaluations.
papers.key_findings:
Models perform best on English-speaking culture questions, even when asked in other languages.
Models exhibit Cultural-Linguistic Synergy: better performance when questions are posed in the language corresponding to the cultural context.
A higher proportion of language-specialized neurons are activated when the cultural context aligns with the language, explaining the synergy.
The proportion of specialized neurons can be used as an indicator for comparing multilingual capabilities during training.
The number of activated neurons is strongly correlated with model performance in the corresponding language.
papers.limitation:
The framework requires dual-format question content for robust cross-cultural comparisons, which may not always be available.
The study focuses on a single cultural context per language, not capturing the diversity within languages spoken in multiple regions.
Interpretability probing is limited to smaller models (e.g., 7B and 8B parameters) due to computational constraints.
future_direction: Expand the framework to incorporate more varied cultural contexts for each language.
Extend interpretability analysis to larger models with more parameters.
Further expand the framework for more comprehensive evaluations of multilingual models.
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a Dual Evaluation Framework to comprehensively assess the multilingual capabilities of LLMs. By decomposing the evaluation along the dimensions of linguistic medium and cultural context, this framework enables a nuanced analysis of LLMs' ability to process questions within both native and cross-cultural contexts cross-lingually. Extensive evaluations are conducted on a wide range of models, revealing a notable "CulturalLinguistic Synergy" phenomenon, where models exhibit better performance when questions are culturally aligned with the language. This phenomenon is further explored through interpretability probing, which shows that a higher proportion of specific neurons are activated in a language's cultural context. This activation proportion could serve as a potential indicator for evaluating multilingual performance during model training. Our findings challenge the prevailing notion that LLMs, primarily trained on English data, perform uniformly across languages and highlight the necessity of culturally and linguistically model evaluations. Our code can be found at https://yingjiahao14. github.io/Dual-Evaluation/.

papers.title: Beyond the Rosetta Stone: Unification Forces in Generalization Dynamics
papers.research_question: What causes cross-lingual factual errors in language models, and how can we understand and improve cross-lingual transfer?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a controlled 'Petri dish' methodology to study cross-lingual knowledge transfer dynamics, identifies a crucial early phase where models develop unified or separate representations across languages, and shows that unification predicts cross-lingual generalization.
papers.conclusion: Controlled settings can shed light on pre-training dynamics and suggest new directions for improving cross-lingual transfer in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Models undergo an early learning phase where they develop either unified or separate representations for the same facts across languages.
Unification of representations is essential for cross-lingual factual transfer.
The degree of unification depends on the mutual information between facts and training data language, and on how easy it is to extract the language feature.
Cross-lingual transfer can be improved without increasing parallel data by manipulating data distribution and tokenization to reduce the language feature's representational footprint.
A unification score, measuring similarity of representations across languages, strongly predicts cross-lingual factual recall accuracy.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) struggle with cross-lingual knowledge transfer: they hallucinate when asked in one language about facts expressed in a different language during training. This work introduces a controlled setting to study the causes and dynamics of this phenomenon by training small Transformer models from scratch on synthetic multilingual datasets. We identify a learning phase wherein a model develops either separate or unified representations of the same facts across languages, and show that unification is essential for cross-lingual transfer. We also show that the degree of unification depends on mutual information between facts and training data language, and on how easy it is to extract that language. Based on these insights, we develop methods to modulate the level of cross-lingual transfer by manipulating data distribution and tokenization, and we introduce metrics and visualizations to formally characterize their effects on unification. Our work shows how controlled settings can shed light on pre-training dynamics and suggests new directions for improving cross-lingual transfer in LLMs.

papers.title: Representing the bilingual's two lexicons
papers.research_question: Does the separation of lexical representations in bilinguals arise from functional independence in a single neural network rather than from architecturally separate systems?
papers.core_contribution: A single neural network can acquire and represent two languages functionally independently, with separation driven by language-specific input and inter-language similarity, without requiring architecturally separate systems.
papers.conclusion: The single network model provides a functional account of bilingual lexical representation and acquisition, explaining empirical data without innate architectural assumptions and accounting for similarity and frequency effects.
papers.key_findings:
A single network can store two lexicons even with sequential training, avoiding catastrophic interference when sufficient language-specific information is provided.
Functional independence of lexical representations in a single network depends on inter-language similarity, with more similar words showing less independence.
Within-language frequency effects can be observed in a single network, simulating human data previously taken as evidence for separate lexicons.
The model accounts for bilingual priming data, including effects of word similarity and frequency.
Second language learning in a single network does not require architecturally separate systems and can generalize within languages.
papers.abstract: A review of empirical work suggests that the lexical representations of a bilingual's two languages are independent (Smith, 1991), but may also be sensitive to between language similarity patterns (e.g. Cristoffanini, Kirsner, and Mi lech, 1986). Some researchers hold that infant bilinguals do not initially differentiate between their two languages (e.g. Redlinger &amp; Park, 1980). Yet by the age of two they appear to have acquired separate linguistic systems for each language (Lanza, 1992). This paper explores the hypothesis that the separation of lexical representations in biUnguals is a functional rather than an architectural one. It suggests that the separation may be driven by differences in the structure of the input to a comm o n architectural system. Connectionist simulations are presented modelling the representation of two sets of lexical information. These simulations explore the conditions required to create functionally independent lexical representations in a single neural network. It is shown that a single network may acquire a second language after learning a first (avoiding the traditional problem of catastrophic interference in these networks). Further it is shown that in a single network, the functional independence of representations is dependent on inter-language similarity patterns. The latter finding is difficult to account for in a model that postulates architecturally separate lexical representations.

papers.title: Compositional Processing Emerges in Neural Networks Solving Math Problems
papers.research_question: Do deep neural networks evaluate arithmetic expressions using the principle of compositionality by encoding and combining partial results?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks trained on math problems can encode partial results of sub-expressions in their internal representations, demonstrating emergent compositional processing.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks can exhibit compositional processing when trained on math problems, though imperfectly, suggesting a blend of compositional and holistic strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Models encode digit quantities in their representations, with vectors organized by numerical value.
Operators encode intermediate arithmetic results, with vector distances correlating with value differences.
These encodings are found in attention vectors, indicating compositional processing.
Compositionality is imperfect, as shown by non-zero correlations across sequences.
Both standard and TP-Transformers exhibit similar patterns of compositional encoding.
papers.limitation:
The observed compositionality is imperfect, with non-zero correlations indicating incomplete separation of sub-expressions.
Models show poor generalization on extrapolation problems with different surface features.
future_direction: Clarify whether scaling leads to human-level compositionality or if explicit design is needed.
papers.abstract: A longstanding question in cognitive science concerns the learning mechanisms underlying compositionality in human cognition. Humans can infer the structured relationships (e.g., grammatical rules) implicit in their sensory observations (e.g., auditory speech), and use this knowledge to guide the composition of simpler meanings into complex wholes. Recent progress in artificial neural networks has shown that when large models are trained on enough linguistic data, grammatical structure emerges in their representations. We extend this work to the domain of mathematical reasoning, where it is possible to formulate precise hypotheses about how meanings (e.g., the quantities corresponding to numerals) should be composed according to structured rules (e.g., order of operations). Our work shows that neural networks are not only able to infer something about the structured relationships implicit in their training data, but can also deploy this knowledge to guide the composition of individual meanings into composite wholes.

papers.title: Evidence from fMRI Supports a Two-Phase Abstraction Process in Language Models
papers.research_question: Why are intermediate layers of LLMs, rather than output layers, most predictive of brain activity? Is this due to the abstraction/composition process or the next-token prediction objective?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that the similarity between LLM representations and brain activity is driven by the abstraction/composition process within LLMs, not by their next-token prediction objective. This is supported by a strong correlation between layerwise encoding performance and the intrinsic dimensionality of representations.
papers.conclusion: The abstraction process in LLMs, characterized by increasing intrinsic dimensionality in intermediate layers, is supported by evidence from fMRI encoding models and is the primary driver of brain-model similarity, rather than the next-token prediction objective.
papers.key_findings:
Encoding performance for predicting brain activity and the intrinsic dimensionality (Id) of layer representations are highly correlated across layers and model sizes.
A two-phase process exists in LLMs: an early abstraction/composition phase (where Id and encoding performance increase) followed by a later prediction phase (where Id decreases and next-token prediction loss drops sharply).
The peak of encoding performance and Id shifts to earlier layers as training progresses, indicating the abstraction phase becomes more compressed.
The relationship between encoding performance and Id emerges during training and is not a trivial function of architecture or layer index.
Brain regions involved in higher-level linguistic processing show a stronger correlation between encoding performance and Id than low-level auditory cortex.
papers.limitation:
The study only tests two model families (OPT and Pythia), so conclusions may not generalize to all LLMs.
It is inherently challenging to draw affirmative conclusions about underlying brain mechanisms from brain-model similarity alone.
future_direction: Test the findings on more model families to establish generalizability.
Explore methods to combine representations from different layers to create a representation with higher intrinsic dimensionality and potentially better encoding performance.
papers.abstract: Research has repeatedly demonstrated that intermediate hidden states extracted from large language models are able to predict measured brain response to natural language stimuli. Yet, very little is known about the representation properties that enable this high prediction performance. Why is it the intermediate layers, and not the output layers, that are most capable for this unique and highly general transfer task? In this work, we show that evidence from language encoding models in fMRI supports the existence of a two-phase abstraction process within LLMs. We use manifold learning methods to show that this abstraction process naturally arises over the course of training a language model and that the first "composition" phase of this abstraction process is compressed into fewer layers as training continues. Finally, we demonstrate a strong correspondence between layerwise encoding performance and the intrinsic dimensionality of representations from LLMs. We give initial evidence that this correspondence primarily derives from the inherent compositionality of LLMs and not their next-word prediction properties.

papers.title: Conceptual structure coheres in human cognition but not in large language models
papers.research_question: Does conceptual structure in large language models cohere across different probing tasks as it does in humans, or do human and LLM conceptual representations differ in robustness?
papers.core_contribution: Human conceptual structure is robust across different tasks and cultures, but large language models exhibit less coherence in conceptual structure across different probing tasks, indicating a lack of a stable conceptual core.
papers.conclusion: Human conceptual structure is robust to differences in task, language, and culture, while contemporary LLMs lack such coherence, highlighting a fundamental difference between human cognition and current machine language models.
papers.key_findings:
Human conceptual structure estimates from three different tasks (feature listing, triadic comparisons, pairwise ratings) are highly coherent (squared Procrustes correlations between 0.72 and 0.96).
LLM conceptual structure estimates vary depending on the probing task; for GPT-3, the squared Procrustes correlations between different task embeddings are lower (e.g., 0.72 between feature listing and triplet, 0.47 between feature listing and pairwise, 0.25 between triplet and pairwise).
LLM conceptual structure from verified feature lists aligns moderately well with human feature norms (squared Procrustes correlation 0.89), but other LLM-derived embeddings align less well.
Chain-of-thought prompting improves alignment with human conceptual structure for some models but does not achieve human-level coherence.
Embeddings from internal representations (e.g., GPT-3 hidden layers, word2vec, CLIP) do not cohere well with each other or with human embeddings.
papers.limitation:
The study uses a constrained set of 30 concepts from two domains; a larger scale study might reveal different results.
The LLM simulations did not employ advanced prompting techniques like tree-of-thought or self-consistency, which might improve coherence.
LLMs lack multimodal sensory experience that humans have, which might affect conceptual organization.
future_direction: Conduct a larger scale study on larger concept sets.
Investigate the use of advanced prompting techniques (e.g., tree-of-thought, self-consistency) to improve conceptual coherence in LLMs.
papers.abstract: Neural network models of language have long been used as a tool for developing hypotheses about conceptual representation in the mind and brain. For many years, such use involved extracting vector-space representations of words and using distances among these to predict or understand human behavior in various semantic tasks. Contemporary large language models (LLMs), however, make it possible to interrogate the latent structure of conceptual representations using experimental methods nearly identical to those commonly used with human participants. The current work utilizes three common techniques borrowed from cognitive psychology to estimate and compare the structure of concepts in humans and a suite of LLMs. In humans, we show that conceptual structure is robust to differences in culture, language, and method of estimation. Structures estimated from LLM behavior, while individually fairly consistent with those estimated from human behavior, vary much more depending upon the particular task used to generate responses--across tasks, estimates of conceptual structure from the very same model cohere less with one another than do human structure estimates. These results highlight an important difference between contemporary LLMs and human cognition, with implications for understanding some fundamental limitations of contemporary machine language.

papers.title: From Passive to Persuasive: Steering Emotional Nuance in Human-AI Negotiation
papers.research_question: Whether complex social behaviors, such as empathy and strategic politeness, are encoded as localized, approximately linear directions in LLM activation space and can be effectively steered via attribution-guided activation injection.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces STAR, a two-stage inference-time framework that uses attribution patching to localize where behavioral traits causally originate and injects contrastive activation vectors at those positions. It demonstrates that complex interpersonal behaviors are encoded as localized, linear directions in activation space and can be effectively steered.
papers.conclusion: The findings indicate that complex interpersonal stances are recoverable as precise, localized directions in residual stream space, and that the central challenge in behavioral alignment is identifying where behavioral intent is encoded, not model capacity.
papers.key_findings:
Localized activation injection (STAR) consistently outperforms global steering and instruction priming across emotional dialogue and negotiation tasks.
Steering effects persist and can compound across multi-turn interactions, with larger effect sizes than in single-turn settings.
Human evaluation confirms that automatic metric gains reflect genuine improvements in perceived conversational quality, not superficial lexical changes.
Attribution patching reveals that behavioral traits localize to specific early-layer attention and MLP components, with distinct patterns for affective vs. strategic tasks.
The work challenges the assumption that complex, context-dependent social behaviors resist linear decomposition in activation space.
papers.limitation: Failure modes include verbatim self-repetition, context mismatch, and register over-inflation where affective framing is applied disproportionately.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate increasing conversational fluency, yet instilling them with nuanced, human-like emotional expression remains a significant challenge. Current alignment techniques often address surface-level output or require extensive fine-tuning. This paper demonstrates that targeted activation engineering can steer LLaMA 3.1-8B to exhibit more human-like emotional nuances. We first employ attribution patching to identify causally influential components, to find a key intervention locus by observing activation patterns during diagnostic conversational tasks. We then derive emotional expression vectors from the difference in the activations generated by contrastive text pairs (positive vs. negative examples of target emotions). Applying these vectors to new conversational prompts significantly enhances emotional characteristics: steered responses show increased positive sentiment (e.g., joy, trust) and more frequent first-person pronoun usage, indicative of greater personal engagement. Our findings offer a precise and interpretable framework and new directions for the study of conversational AI.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Propositional Logical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform propositional logical reasoning? What computational strategies do they employ?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning in Qwen3 models, comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation, Information Transmission, Fact Retrospection, and Specialized Attention Heads.
papers.conclusion: The investigation uncovers a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning, with four interlocking mechanisms that generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, suggesting fundamental computational strategies rather than task-specific shortcuts.
papers.key_findings:
The model organizes reasoning into staged computation: early layers process facts, middle layers process logical expressions, and late layers aggregate for prediction.
Information transmission occurs through segment-terminal tokens (boundary tokens) that act as information hubs.
Fact retrospection: the model persistently re-accesses source fact tokens throughout the network depth.
Specialized attention heads: splitting heads (early layers), transmission heads (middle layers), and fact-retrieval heads (middle to late layers) implement the above mechanisms.
These mechanisms generalize across model scales (8B and 14B), rule types (11 categories), and reasoning depths (one-hop and two-hop).
papers.limitation:
The internal computations within MLP layers remain largely unexplored.
The analysis does not explain how or when these mechanisms emerge during training.
Cannot definitively rule out that these patterns reflect sophisticated statistical shortcuts rather than genuine logical algorithms.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to deeper reasoning chains (i.e., three-hop and beyond).
Investigating diverse model architectures beyond the Qwen family (e.g., Llama, Mistral, etc.).
Analyzing training dynamics to reveal how and when these mechanisms emerge during pretraining.
papers.abstract: Understanding how Large Language Models (LLMs) perform logical reasoning internally remains a fundamental challenge. While prior mechanistic studies focus on identifying taskspecific circuits, they leave open the question of what computational strategies LLMs employ for propositional reasoning. We address this gap through comprehensive analysis of Qwen3 (8B and 14B) on PropLogic-MI, a controlled dataset spanning 11 propositional logic rule categories across one-hop and two-hop reasoning. Rather than asking ''which components are necessary,'' we ask ''how does the model organize computation?'' Our analysis reveals a coherent computational architecture comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation (layer-wise processing phases), Information Transmission (information flow aggregation at boundary tokens), Fact Retrospection (persistent re-access of source facts), and Specialized Attention Heads (functionally distinct head types). These mechanisms generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, providing mechanistic evidence that LLMs employ structured computational strategies for logical reasoning.

papers.title: Understanding Cross-Lingual Syntactic Transfer in Multilingual Recurrent Neural Networks.
papers.research_question: Does exposure to a related language (L1) improve implicit syntactic knowledge in a target language (L2) within multilingual neural networks? Do these networks induce a common representation space with shared syntactic categories?
papers.core_contribution: Cross-lingual syntactic transfer in multilingual neural networks is limited and inconsistent, and optimal conditions for lexical-semantic transfer may not be optimal for syntactic transfer.
papers.conclusion: Transfer of purely grammatical knowledge is limited and dependent on language pairs, and modern multilingual neural networks are still far from acquiring a true interlingua.
papers.key_findings:
Exposing a model to a related language does not always improve grammatical knowledge in the target language; in some cases, it causes negative interference.
Transfer of purely grammatical knowledge (e.g., long-range agreement in nonce sentences) is very limited and strongly dependent on the specific source-target language pair.
Part-of-speech categories are shared to a moderate extent across languages in the models, but dependency categories are not shared at all.
Language relatedness is the most determining factor for both word embedding alignment and part-of-speech transfer.
Scaling from two to nine input languages improves part-of-speech transfer among related languages but worsens it between unrelated languages.
papers.limitation:
Transfer of syntactic knowledge is limited and inconsistent, with negative interference observed in some language pairs (e.g., French to Italian).
Syntactic knowledge transfer within the models is shallow, with dependency categories not shared across languages.
papers.abstract: It is now established that modern neural language models can be successfully trained on multiple languages simultaneously without changes to the underlying architecture. But what kind of knowledge is really shared among languages within these models? Does multilingual training mostly lead to an alignment of the lexical representation spaces or does it also enable the sharing of purely grammatical knowledge? In this paper we dissect different forms of cross-lingual transfer and look for its most determining factors, using a variety of models and probing tasks. We find that exposing our LMs to a related language does not always increase grammatical knowledge in the target language, and that optimal conditions for lexical-semantic transfer may not be optimal for syntactic transfer.

papers.title: Among Us: A Sandbox for Measuring and Detecting Agentic Deception
papers.research_question: How can we elicit, measure, and detect open-ended, long-term agentic deception in LLM-agents using a sandbox environment?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Among Us sandbox and Deception Elo metric to study open-ended agentic deception, and shows that frontier models are better at deception than detection, while linear probes can detect deception out-of-distribution.
papers.conclusion: The Among Us sandbox and Deception Elo metric provide a valuable environment for studying agentic deception, and interpretability techniques like linear probes are effective for out-of-distribution deception detection, contributing to AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
Frontier reasoning models are differentially better at producing deception than at detecting it.
Linear probes trained on dishonesty datasets (e.g., RepEng, DishonestQA) generalize extremely well to detect deception in the Among Us sandbox, achieving AUROCs over 95%.
Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features can detect deception out-of-distribution but are ineffective for steering models to lie less.
The Among Us sandbox successfully elicits open-ended, long-term deceptive behavior from LLM-agents without fine-tuning or in-context examples.
Models trained with reinforcement learning (RL) are comparatively much better at producing deception than detecting it.
papers.limitation:
The results might not represent real-world user-model interaction, or the deception mechanisms in the sandbox could differ from real-world settings.
The techniques might work for uninteresting reasons (e.g., detecting impostor/crewmate tokens based on latent knowledge associations).
Potential failure mode of sandbagging, where models strategically underperform.
Models likely have prior knowledge of Among Us from pre-training, which may influence behavior.
future_direction: Conduct more experiments with different models and safety techniques, including responsible human trials.
Train models for deception in the controlled sandbox to study generalization and superhuman capabilities.
Explore other model organisms and sandboxes for studying deception, including more real-world scenarios and games that decouple deception from fixed role assignment.
papers.abstract: Prior studies on deception in language-based AI agents typically assess whether the agent produces a false statement about a topic, or makes a binary choice prompted by a goal, rather than allowing open-ended deceptive behavior to emerge in pursuit of a longer-term goal. To fix this, we introduce Among Us, a sandbox social deception game where LLM-agents exhibit long-term, open-ended deception as a consequence of the game objectives. While most benchmarks saturate quickly, Among Us can be expected to last much longer, because it is a multi-player game far from equilibrium. Using the sandbox, we evaluate 18 proprietary and open-weight LLMs and uncover a general trend: models trained with RL are comparatively much better at producing deception than detecting it. We evaluate the effectiveness of methods to detect lying and deception: logistic regression on the activations and sparse autoencoders (SAEs). We find that probes trained on a dataset of "pretend you're a dishonest model:.." generalize extremely well out-of-distribution, consistently obtaining AUROCs over 95% even when evaluated just on the deceptive statement, without the chain of thought. We also find two SAE features that work well at deception detection but are unable to steer the model to lie less. We hope our open-sourced sandbox, game logs, and probes serve to anticipate and mitigate deceptive behavior and capabilities in language-based agents.

papers.title: Mind Scramble: Unveiling Large Language Model Psychology Via Typoglycemia
papers.research_question: Does LLM possess human-like cognitive processes and mechanisms in reading and comprehending? The paper uses Typoglycemia to explore this.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces LLM Psychology, a framework that uses Typoglycemia experiments to study cognitive behaviors of LLMs. It finds that LLMs exhibit human-like behaviors but are fundamentally data-driven, and each LLM has a unique cognitive pattern.
papers.conclusion: The study advances research on aligning LLMs with human cognition and provides evidence that LLMs' abilities are data-driven, offering a case for LLM Psychology.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as slightly lower task accuracy with consuming more tokens and time.
Different LLMs show varying degrees of robustness to scrambled input, making it a democratized benchmark for model evaluation.
The impact of different task types varies, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) in scrambled format being more challenging.
LLMs' emergent human-like abilities are fundamentally statistical and data-driven, rather than genuinely resembling human cognition.
Each LLM exhibits its unique and consistent 'cognitive pattern' across various tasks, unveiling a general mechanism in its psychology process.
papers.abstract: Research into the external behaviors and internal mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) has shown promise in addressing complex tasks in the physical world. Studies suggest that powerful LLMs, like GPT-4, are beginning to exhibit human-like cognitive abilities, including planning, reasoning, and reflection. In this paper, we introduce a research line and methodology called LLM Psychology, leveraging human psychology experiments to investigate the cognitive behaviors and mechanisms of LLMs. We migrate the Typoglycemia phenomenon from psychology to explore the "mind" of LLMs. Unlike human brains, which rely on context and word patterns to comprehend scrambled text, LLMs use distinct encoding and decoding processes. Through Typoglycemia experiments at the character, word, and sentence levels, we observe: (I) LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as lower task accuracy and higher token/time consumption; (II) LLMs exhibit varying robustness to scrambled input, making Typoglycemia a benchmark for model evaluation without new datasets; (III) Different task types have varying impacts, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) being more challenging in scrambled form; (IV) Each LLM has a unique and consistent "cognitive pattern" across tasks, revealing general mechanisms in its psychology process. We provide an in-depth analysis of hidden layers to explain these phenomena, paving the way for future research in LLM Psychology and deeper interpretability.

papers.title: What Does Loss Optimization Actually Teach, If Anything? Knowledge Dynamics in Continual Pre-training of LLMs
papers.research_question: How does loss optimization during continual pre-training (CPT) relate to the acquisition and retention of factual knowledge in LLMs, and does it provide a reliable signal for learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that loss optimization is misaligned with knowledge acquisition in continual pre-training (CPT); factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic despite monotonic loss decrease, and circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of internal knowledge pathways.
papers.conclusion: Loss optimization is not a reliable indicator of learning in CPT; probe-based trajectories reveal narrow learning windows invisible to loss curves, motivating task-based stopping criteria.
papers.key_findings:
Optimization and learning systematically diverge: loss decreases monotonically while factual knowledge acquisition is unstable and non-monotonic.
Acquired facts are rarely consolidated; learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure (entity frequency).
Out-of-domain (OOD) task performance degrades from early epochs during CPT.
Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, explaining narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) provides a much higher upper bound for factual recall, indicating the limitation is in the optimization process, not the data.
future_direction: Novel training objectives, evaluation protocols, and diagnostic tools that make learning dynamics observable during model adaptation.
Task-based stopping criteria that rely on task-level performance rather than next-token prediction.
papers.abstract: Continual Pre-Training (CPT) is widely used for acquiring and updating factual knowledge in LLMs. This practice treats loss as a proxy for knowledge learning, while offering no grounding into how it changes during training. We study CPT as a knowledge learning process rather than a solely optimization problem. We construct a controlled, distribution-matched benchmark of factual documents and interleave diagnostic probes directly into the CPT loop, enabling epoch-level measurement of knowledge acquisition dynamics and changes in Out-Of-Domain (OOD) general skills (e.g., math). We further analyze how CPT reshapes knowledge circuits during training. Across three instruction-tuned LLMs and multiple CPT strategies, optimization and learning systematically diverge as loss decreases monotonically while factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic. Acquired facts are rarely consolidated, learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure, and OOD performance degrades from early epochs. Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, providing an explanation for narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting. These results show that loss optimization is misaligned with learning progress in CPT and motivate evaluation of stopping criteria based on task-level learning dynamics.

papers.title: CRANE: Causal Relevance Analysis of Language-Specific Neurons in Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How are language capabilities organized at the neuron level in multilingual LLMs? The paper redefines language specificity in terms of functional necessity and proposes a method to identify language-specific neurons.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CRANE, a relevance-based framework for identifying language-specific neurons by functional necessity, and finds asymmetric, language-selective but non-exclusive neuron specializations in multilingual LLMs.
papers.conclusion: CRANE provides a framework for studying language-specific neurons based on functional necessity, revealing that language-specific neurons are language-selective but non-exclusive, and highlighting the importance of distinguishing statistical correlation from functional contribution.
papers.key_findings:
CRANE induces targeted functional degradation on the intended language while preserving performance on non-target languages, outperforming activation-based methods like LAPE.
Neuron-level interventions reveal an asymmetric pattern: masking neurons relevant to a target language selectively degrades performance on that language while preserving performance on other languages, indicating language-selective but non-exclusive neuron specializations.
Normalized kurtosis of relevance distributions reveals language-related structure in neuron contributions.
Neuron sets identified on the Base model retain functional influence when transferred to the Chat model, indicating partial preservation of language-specific neurons after instruction tuning.
The proposed LangSpec-F1 metric quantifies language-selective functional effects under neuron intervention.
papers.limitation:
CRANE currently relies on normalized kurtosis to characterize concentration patterns in language-conditioned relevance distributions, which is only one possible statistic.
Functional validation is performed via neuron masking, a relatively coarse intervention; more fine-grained causal techniques may provide deeper insight.
Experiments focus on three languages and a single model family, and open-ended generation evaluation uses an LLM-as-a-judge protocol which may introduce variance.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to broader language coverage, additional architectures, and alternative evaluation paradigms.
Using more fine-grained causal techniques, such as neuron re-weighting or path-specific analysis.
papers.abstract: Multilingual large language models (LLMs) achieve strong performance across languages, yet how language capabilities are organized at the neuron level remains poorly understood. Prior work has identified language-related neurons mainly through activation-based heuristics, which conflate language preference with functional importance. Prior work has identified language-related neurons mainly through activation-based heuristics, which conflate language preference with functional importance. We propose CRANE, a relevance-based analysis framework that redefines language specificity in terms of functional necessity, identifying language-specific neurons through targeted neuron-level interventions. CRANE characterizes neuron specialization by their contribution to language-conditioned predictions rather than activation magnitude. Our implementation will be made publicly available. Neuron-level interventions reveal a consistent asymmetric pattern: masking neurons relevant to a target language selectively degrades performance on that language while preserving performance on other languages to a substantial extent, indicating language-selective but non-exclusive neuron specializations. Experiments on English, Chinese, and Vietnamese across multiple benchmarks, together with a dedicated relevance-based metric and base-to-chat model transfer analysis, show that CRANE isolates language-specific components more precisely than activation-based methods.

papers.title: Behind the Scene: Revealing the Secrets of Pre-trained Vision-and-Language Models
papers.research_question: How do pre-trained vision-and-language models work internally? Specifically, the paper investigates multimodal fusion, modality importance, cross-modal interaction, visual relations, and linguistic knowledge in these models.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces VALUE, a set of probing tasks for vision-and-language models, and uses it to analyze UNITER and LXMERT, revealing that textual modality is more dominant, a subset of heads specialize in cross-modal interaction, and visual relations and linguistic knowledge are encoded.
papers.conclusion: The analysis provides insights into the inner workings of pre-trained V+L models and offers guidelines for future model design, such as preferring single-stream architecture and initializing with BERT weights.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-trained models attend more to text than images during inference.
A subset of attention heads are tailored for capturing cross-modal interactions.
Learned attention matrices show patterns coherent with latent alignment between image regions and textual words.
Attention patterns reveal visually-interpretable relations among image regions.
Linguistic knowledge is effectively encoded in the attention heads.
future_direction: Perform model compression via pruning attention heads based on the analysis.
papers.abstract: Recent Transformer-based large-scale pre-trained models have revolutionized vision-and-language (V+L) research. Models such as ViLBERT, LXMERT and UNITER have significantly lifted state of the art across a wide range of V+L benchmarks with joint image-text pre-training. However, little is known about the inner mechanisms that destine their impressive success. To reveal the secrets behind the scene of these powerful models, we present VALUE (Vision-And-Language Understanding Evaluation), a set of meticulously designed probing tasks (e.g., Visual Coreference Resolution, Visual Relation Detection, Linguistic Probing Tasks) generalizable to standard pre-trained V+L models, aiming to decipher the inner workings of multimodal pre-training (e.g., the implicit knowledge garnered in individual attention heads, the inherent cross-modal alignment learned through contextualized multimodal embeddings). Through extensive analysis of each archetypal model architecture via these probing tasks, our key observations are: (i) Pre-trained models exhibit a propensity for attending over text rather than images during inference. (ii) There exists a subset of attention heads that are tailored for capturing cross-modal interactions. (iii) Learned attention matrix in pre-trained models demonstrates patterns coherent with the latent alignment between image regions and textual words. (iv) Plotted attention patterns reveal visually-interpretable relations among image regions. (v) Pure linguistic knowledge is also effectively encoded in the attention heads. These are valuable insights serving to guide future work towards designing better model architecture and objectives for multimodal pre-training.

papers.title: One Mind, Many Tongues: A Deep Dive into Language-Agnostic Knowledge Neurons in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we accurately localize language-agnostic knowledge neurons in large language models, considering uncertainty across queries and languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces MATRICE, a method for localizing language-agnostic knowledge neurons by quantifying uncertainty across queries and languages, and constructs the RML-LAMA benchmark. It demonstrates these neurons' roles in cross-lingual editing, knowledge enhancement, and injection.
papers.conclusion: The proposed MATRICE method accurately localizes language-agnostic knowledge neurons, and these neurons are shown to be conducive to cross-lingual knowledge editing, enhancement, and injection.
papers.key_findings:
A significant proportion of language-agnostic knowledge neurons are distributed in the last few layers of LLMs.
Manipulating (suppressing/enhancing) language-agnostic knowledge neurons significantly affects knowledge expression across languages.
A single edit on language-agnostic knowledge neurons can simultaneously modify corresponding knowledge in all languages (cross-lingual editing).
Amplifying the activation of language-agnostic knowledge neurons improves prediction performance in low-resource languages.
Fine-tuning only parameters associated with language-agnostic knowledge neurons helps LLMs learn new knowledge while alleviating forgetting of old knowledge.
