Despite the recent success of deep neural networks in natural language
processing (NLP), their interpretability remains a challenge. We analyze the
representations learned by neural machine translation models at various levels
of granularity and evaluate their quality through relevant extrinsic
properties. In particular, we seek answers to the following questions: (i) How
accurately is word-structure captured within the learned representations, an
important aspect in translating morphologically-rich languages? (ii) Do the
representations capture long-range dependencies, and effectively handle
syntactically divergent languages? (iii) Do the representations capture lexical
semantics? We conduct a thorough investigation along several parameters: (i)
Which layers in the architecture capture each of these linguistic phenomena;
(ii) How does the choice of translation unit (word, character, or subword unit)
impact the linguistic properties captured by the underlying representations?
(iii) Do the encoder and decoder learn differently and independently? (iv) Do
the representations learned by multilingual NMT models capture the same amount
of linguistic information as their bilingual counterparts? Our data-driven,
quantitative evaluation illuminates important aspects in NMT models and their
ability to capture various linguistic phenomena. We show that deep NMT models
learn a non-trivial amount of linguistic information. Notable findings include:
i) Word morphology and part-of-speech information are captured at the lower
layers of the model; (ii) In contrast, lexical semantics or non-local syntactic
and semantic dependencies are better represented at the higher layers; (iii)
Representations learned using characters are more informed about wordmorphology
compared to those learned using subword units; and (iv) Representations learned
by multilingual models are richer compared to bilingual models.

papers.title: Do LLMs Need Inherent Reasoning Before Reinforcement Learning? A Study in Korean Self-Correction
papers.research_question: Can LLMs enhance their Korean reasoning abilities through reinforcement learning to a level comparable to English, and is having inherent Korean reasoning capabilities necessary for RL to be effective?
papers.core_contribution: Aligning language-specific neurons in early layers enhances internal translation, enabling reinforcement learning to effectively improve Korean reasoning and self-correction in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: The key to improving multilingual reasoning in LLMs is not injecting new capabilities in low-resource languages, but effectively eliciting and aligning the model's existing reasoning abilities through strategic neuron-level interventions.
papers.key_findings:
RL alone yields limited improvements for Korean reasoning without inherent Korean reasoning capabilities.
Tuning Korean-specific neurons in early layers significantly improves Korean reasoning and self-correction performance.
After neuron tuning, RL becomes much more effective in enhancing Korean reasoning.
The generation difficulty for Korean mathematical reasoning and self-correction is higher than for English.
Deactivating Korean-specific neurons in early layers severely degrades performance on Korean reasoning tasks.
papers.limitation:
Focus on early layers and math/self-correction tasks may not generalize to other domains or languages.
Does not enhance native Korean understanding like fluency or cultural nuance.
Relies on relatively small-scale code-switching data, and scalability in low-resource scenarios is unexplored.
Validation is limited to select LLM architectures (e.g., LLaMA and Qwen).
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate strong reasoning and self-correction abilities in high-resource languages like English, but their performance remains limited in low-resource languages such as Korean. In this study, we investigate whether reinforcement learning (RL) can enhance Korean reasoning abilities to a degree comparable to English. Our findings reveal that RL alone yields limited improvements when applied to models lacking inherent Korean reasoning capabilities. To address this, we explore several fine-tuning strategies and show that aligning the model's internal reasoning processes with Korean inputs-particularly by tuning Korean-specific neurons in early layers-is key to unlocking RL's effectiveness. We introduce a self-correction code-switching dataset to facilitate this alignment and observe significant performance gains in both mathematical reasoning and self-correction tasks. Ultimately, we conclude that the crucial factor in multilingual reasoning enhancement is not injecting new linguistic knowledge, but effectively eliciting and aligning existing reasoning capabilities. Our study provides a new perspective on how internal translation and neuron-level tuning contribute to multilingual reasoning alignment in LLMs.

papers.title: Analyzing LLMs' Knowledge Boundary Cognition Across Languages Through the Lens of Internal Representations
papers.research_question: How do LLMs recognize knowledge boundaries across different languages, and can this ability be transferred or enhanced?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes how LLMs perceive knowledge boundaries across languages, finds that this perception is encoded in middle layers with linear structure, and proposes training-free alignment and fine-tuning methods to transfer and enhance this ability.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals that LLMs encode knowledge boundary cognition in middle layers with linear structure, enabling cross-lingual transfer through training-free alignment and fine-tuning, providing insights and methods for improving hallucination reduction in low-resource languages.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge boundary cognition is encoded in the middle to middle-upper layers of LLMs across languages.
Language differences in knowledge boundary perception follow a linear structure, enabling training-free alignment methods like mean-shifting and linear projection.
Training-free methods effectively transfer knowledge boundary perception across languages, reducing the performance gap.
Fine-tuning on bilingual question translation data enhances LLMs' recognition of knowledge boundaries across languages.
A weak-to-strong generalization pattern where probes trained on low-resource languages perform better on projected high-resource representations.
papers.limitation: It is difficult to investigate how representations evolve during the generation process, such as in chain-of-thought reasoning, due to challenges in locating when transformations occur.
future_direction: Investigating how knowledge boundary representations evolve during the generation process, especially in long chain-of-thought reasoning.
papers.abstract: While understanding the knowledge boundaries of LLMs is crucial to prevent hallucination, research on the knowledge boundaries of LLMs has predominantly focused on English. In this work, we present the first study to analyze how LLMs recognize knowledge boundaries across different languages by probing their internal representations when processing known and unknown questions in multiple languages. Our empirical studies reveal three key findings: 1) LLMs' perceptions of knowledge boundaries are encoded in the middle to middle-upper layers across different languages. 2) Language differences in knowledge boundary perception follow a linear structure, which motivates our proposal of a training-free alignment method that effectively transfers knowledge boundary perception ability across languages, thereby helping reduce hallucination risk in low-resource languages; 3) Fine-tuning on bilingual question pair translation further enhances LLMs' recognition of knowledge boundaries across languages. Given the absence of standard testbeds for cross-lingual knowledge boundary analysis, we construct a multilingual evaluation suite comprising three representative types of knowledge boundary data. Our code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/DAMO-NLP-SG/LLM-Multilingual-Knowledge-Boundaries.

papers.title: PragWorld: A Benchmark Evaluating LLMs' Local World Model under Minimal Linguistic Alterations and Conversational Dynamics
papers.research_question: Do language models construct an implicit world model of the environment described in the input, and how malleable are these representations under minimal linguistic alterations in conversational contexts?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the PRAGWORLD benchmark to evaluate the malleability of LLMs' internal world models under minimal linguistic alterations in conversations, and proposes a dual-perspective interpretability framework to identify harmful/useful layers and improve robustness via layer-regularization fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals that LLMs have fragile world models that are not robustly accurate under linguistic alterations, but the proposed interpretability framework and regularization techniques can help understand and mitigate these issues.
papers.key_findings:
Language models struggle to maintain robust accuracy under minimal linguistic alterations in conversations, indicating brittleness in their latent world models.
The proposed dual-perspective interpretability framework (using Direct Effect Patching and MLP Zero-Out ablation) can identify transformer layers that encode useful or harmful reasoning patterns.
Fine-tuning models on synthetic data with the proposed regularization techniques (Useful Layer Amplification and Harmful Layer Suppression) improves robust accuracy, especially for smaller models.
Models exhibit a strong bias towards answering 'Yes' or 'No', which is more pronounced in smaller models and persists even after fine-tuning.
Entity tracking ability, i.e., memorizing and updating information about entities in a conversation, improves with model scale and is enhanced by fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Real-world conversations are rich with pragmatic elements, such as entity mentions, references, and implicatures. Understanding such nuances is a requirement for successful natural communication, and often requires building a local world model which encodes such elements and captures the dynamics of their evolving states. However, it is not well-understood whether language models (LMs) construct or maintain a robust implicit representation of conversations. In this work, we evaluate the ability of LMs to encode and update their internal world model in dyadic conversations and test their malleability under linguistic alterations. To facilitate this, we apply seven minimal linguistic alterations to conversations sourced from popular datasets and construct two benchmarks comprising yes-no questions. We evaluate a wide range of open and closed source LMs and observe that they struggle to maintain robust accuracy. Our analysis unveils that LMs struggle to memorize crucial details, such as tracking entities under linguistic alterations to conversations. We then propose a dual-perspective interpretability framework which identifies transformer layers that are useful or harmful and highlights linguistic alterations most influenced by harmful layers, typically due to encoding spurious signals or relying on shortcuts. Inspired by these insights, we propose two layer-regularization based fine-tuning strategies that suppress the effect of the harmful layers.

papers.title: The Rise and Down of Babel Tower: Investigating the Evolution Process of Multilingual Code Large Language Model
papers.research_question: How do the multilingual capabilities of LLMs evolve during the pre-training process?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Babel Tower Hypothesis to explain how LLMs evolve multilingual capabilities during pre-training, and introduces a method to optimize pre-training data distribution for multilingual code LLMs.
papers.conclusion: The Babel Tower Hypothesis explains the evolution of multilingual capabilities in LLMs, and optimizing the pre-training data distribution based on this hypothesis significantly improves multilingual performance.
papers.key_findings:
The performance of a new language during pre-training follows three stages: translation (reliance on dominant language), transition, and stabilization (use of own language-specific system).
For some languages, relying on a strong dominant language for translation is more effective than building a new knowledge system with additional data.
The internal state of the LLM, measured via working languages and language-transferring neurons, shifts from the dominant language system to the new language system over training.
Adjusting the pre-training data distribution allows different languages to reach their optimal performance state concurrently.
A method to estimate the optimal pre-training corpus distribution based on training loss and performance leads to models that outperform those trained on the original corpus.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to code languages and smaller models; future work should extend to natural languages and larger models.
future_direction: Extend the approach to natural language scenarios.
Scale to larger models.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown significant multilingual capabilities. However, the mechanisms underlying the development of these capabilities during pre-training are not well understood. In this paper, we use code LLMs as an experimental platform to explore the evolution of multilingual capabilities in LLMs during the pre-training process. Based on our observations, we propose the Babel Tower Hypothesis, which describes the entire process of LLMs acquiring new language capabilities. During the learning process, multiple languages initially share a single knowledge system dominated by the primary language and gradually develop language-specific knowledge systems. We then validate the above hypothesis by tracking the internal states of the LLMs through identifying working languages and language transferring neurons. Experimental results show that the internal state changes of the LLM are consistent with our Babel Tower Hypothesis. Building on these insights, we propose a novel method to construct an optimized pre-training corpus for multilingual code LLMs, which significantly outperforms LLMs trained on the original corpus. The proposed Babel Tower Hypothesis provides new insights into designing pre-training data distributions to achieve optimal multilingual capabilities in LLMs.

papers.title: How does GPT-2 compute greater-than?: Interpreting mathematical abilities in a pre-trained language model
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 compute the greater-than operation in a year-span prediction task?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies and explains a circuit in GPT-2 small responsible for computing the greater-than operation in a year-span prediction task, showing it activates across diverse contexts.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a detailed circuit-level explanation of a mathematical ability in a pre-trained LM, laying groundwork for future work on memorization and generalization in larger models.
papers.key_findings:
A circuit consisting of specific attention heads and MLPs (8-11) is responsible for the greater-than computation.
Attention heads identify the start year YY and communicate it to downstream MLPs.
MLPs 9, 10, and 11 compute the greater-than operation, with MLP 10 playing a central role.
The circuit generalizes to other tasks requiring greater-than but also incorrectly activates in some contexts (e.g., less-than tasks).
The mechanism is more complex than simple memorization but does not reflect full mathematical generalization.
papers.limitation:
Limited by the small size of the model (GPT-2 small) and the simple phenomenon studied.
The study is model-centric; data-driven interpretability techniques would strengthen the work.
future_direction: Studying circuit performance across more diverse tasks to better measure generalization.
Studying larger models to confirm if the results hold.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models can be surprisingly adept at tasks they were not explicitly trained on, but how they implement these capabilities is poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the basic mathematical abilities often acquired by pre-trained language models. Concretely, we use mechanistic interpretability techniques to explain the (limited) mathematical abilities of GPT-2 small. As a case study, we examine its ability to take in sentences such as "The war lasted from the year 1732 to the year 17", and predict valid two-digit end years (years > 32). We first identify a circuit, a small subset of GPT-2 small's computational graph that computes this task's output. Then, we explain the role of each circuit component, showing that GPT-2 small's final multi-layer perceptrons boost the probability of end years greater than the start year. Finally, we find related tasks that activate our circuit. Our results suggest that GPT-2 small computes greater-than using a complex but general mechanism that activates across diverse contexts.

papers.title: Reasoning as State Transition: A Representational Analysis of Reasoning Evolution in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does reasoning ability evolve during training in large language models, and what is the role of internal representation dynamics in this process?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a representational analysis framework showing that post-training yields limited improvement in static initial representation quality, but reasoning involves a continuous distributional shift in representations during generation, which post-training enhances to drive representations toward a better state for task solving.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a novel representational perspective on reasoning evolution in LLMs, highlighting the importance of internal state dynamics and the role of post-training in enhancing state transitions, offering insights for future model analysis and optimization.
papers.key_findings:
Post-training yields only limited improvement in static initial representation quality.
Reasoning involves a significant continuous distributional shift in representations during generation, unlike non-reasoning tasks.
Post-training empowers models to drive this representation transition toward a better distribution for task solving.
There is a high correlation between generation correctness and final representations, but low correlation with initial representations.
The semantic content of the generated tokens is the dominant driver of the state transition, not additional computation or intrinsic parameter differences.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have achieved remarkable performance on reasoning tasks, motivating research into how this ability evolves during training. Prior work has primarily analyzed this evolution via explicit generation outcomes, treating the reasoning process as a black box and obscuring internal changes. To address this opacity, we introduce a representational perspective to investigate the dynamics of the model's internal states. Through comprehensive experiments across models at various training stages, we discover that post-training yields only limited improvement in static initial representation quality. Furthermore, we reveal that, distinct from non-reasoning tasks, reasoning involves a significant continuous distributional shift in representations during generation. Comparative analysis indicates that post-training empowers models to drive this transition toward a better distribution for task solving. To clarify the relationship between internal states and external outputs, statistical analysis confirms a high correlation between generation correctness and the final representations; while counterfactual experiments identify the semantics of the generated tokens, rather than additional computation during inference or intrinsic parameter differences, as the dominant driver of the transition. Collectively, we offer a novel understanding of the reasoning process and the effect of training on reasoning enhancement, providing valuable insights for future model analysis and optimization.

papers.title: Far from the Shallow: Brain-Predictive Reasoning Embedding through Residual Disentanglement
papers.research_question: How can reasoning-specific components in LLM representations be isolated, and how do these isolated reasoning embeddings align with human brain activity during language comprehension?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a residual disentanglement method to isolate reasoning-specific embeddings from LLM hidden states, and uses these embeddings to provide neural evidence for abstract reasoning computations during language comprehension, showing distinct spatiotemporal brain alignment.
papers.conclusion: The work provides compelling neural evidence for an abstract reasoning computation during language comprehension and offers a robust framework for mapping distinct cognitive functions from artificial models to the human brain.
papers.key_findings:
Residual disentanglement yields four nearly orthogonal embeddings for lexicon, syntax, meaning, and reasoning.
The isolated reasoning embedding accounts for unique variance in neural activity not explained by other linguistic features and recruits visual regions beyond classical language areas.
The neural signature for reasoning peaks later (~350-400ms) than signals for lexicon, syntax, and meaning, consistent with a processing hierarchy.
Standard, non-disentangled LLM embeddings are biased toward linguistically shallow features (lexicon, syntax), masking the contributions of deeper cognitive processing like reasoning.
The method provides a framework for mapping distinct cognitive functions from artificial models to the human brain.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on ECoG data provides limited spatial coverage, with insufficient sampling in frontal regions crucial for reasoning.
The role of layers beyond the reasoning saturation layer (around layer 30 in Qwen2.5-14B) remains unclear; they may encode more abstract representations.
future_direction: Integrate complementary modalities such as fMRI to improve spatial resolution.
Explore larger models optimized for multi-step reasoning to reveal stronger or more specialized reasoning signals.
Investigate how higher-level representations in deeper layers (beyond reasoning saturation) might align with cortical hierarchies or large-scale cognitive organization.
papers.abstract: Understanding how the human brain progresses from processing simple linguistic inputs to performing high-level reasoning is a fundamental challenge in neuroscience. While modern large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to model neural responses to language, their internal representations are highly "entangled," mixing information about lexicon, syntax, meaning, and reasoning. This entanglement biases conventional brain encoding analyses toward linguistically shallow features (e.g., lexicon and syntax), making it difficult to isolate the neural substrates of cognitively deeper processes. Here, we introduce a residual disentanglement method that computationally isolates these components. By first probing an LM to identify feature-specific layers, our method iteratively regresses out lower-level representations to produce four nearly orthogonal embeddings for lexicon, syntax, meaning, and, critically, reasoning. We used these disentangled embeddings to model intracranial (ECoG) brain recordings from neurosurgical patients listening to natural speech. We show that: 1) This isolated reasoning embedding exhibits unique predictive power, accounting for variance in neural activity not explained by other linguistic features and even extending to the recruitment of visual regions beyond classical language areas. 2) The neural signature for reasoning is temporally distinct, peaking later (~350-400ms) than signals related to lexicon, syntax, and meaning, consistent with its position atop a processing hierarchy. 3) Standard, non-disentangled LLM embeddings can be misleading, as their predictive success is primarily attributable to linguistically shallow features, masking the more subtle contributions of deeper cognitive processing.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: Disjoint Processing Mechanisms of Hierarchical and Linear Grammars in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) demonstrate distinct, localizable mechanisms for processing hierarchically structured vs. linearly structured sentences that are otherwise superficially identical?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs develop distinct, localizable components for processing hierarchical grammatical structures that are separate from those processing linear structures, and this functional specialization emerges from exposure to language data without human-like inductive biases.
papers.conclusion: Functional specialization toward hierarchical linguistic structure can arise in LLMs solely from exposure to large-scale language distributions, even in the absence of strong human-like inductive biases.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs are more accurate at grammaticality judgments for hierarchical inputs than for linear inputs.
The model components (neurons) causally responsible for processing hierarchical grammars show high overlap with each other but low overlap with those responsible for linear grammars.
Ablating hierarchy-sensitive components significantly reduces accuracy on hierarchical grammars but has a lesser effect on linear grammars, and vice-versa.
Hierarchy-sensitive components identified using natural language are also active and influential when processing grammars constructed from nonce words (Jabberwocky sentences), indicating sensitivity to abstract structure rather than meaning or in-distribution language.
papers.limitation: LLMs are trained on data containing multiple languages, unlike the human subjects in the original study who were fluent only in their native language and tested on unfamiliar ones.
future_direction: Investigating cross-linguistic generalization of hierarchical processing mechanisms.
Exploring the role of scale (model size and dataset size) in the emergence of functional specialization.
papers.abstract: All natural languages are structured hierarchically. In humans, this structural restriction is neurologically coded: when two grammars are presented with identical vocabularies, brain areas responsible for language processing are only sensitive to hierarchical grammars. Using large language models (LLMs), we investigate whether such functionally distinct hierarchical processing regions can arise solely from exposure to large-scale language distributions. We generate inputs using English, Italian, Japanese, or nonce words, varying the underlying grammars to conform to either hierarchical or linear/positional rules. Using these grammars, we first observe that language models show distinct behaviors on hierarchical versus linearly structured inputs. Then, we find that the components responsible for processing hierarchical grammars are distinct from those that process linear grammars; we causally verify this in ablation experiments. Finally, we observe that hierarchy-selective components are also active on nonce grammars; this suggests that hierarchy sensitivity is not tied to meaning, nor in-distribution inputs.

papers.title: Opening the Black Box: A Survey on the Mechanisms of Multi-Step Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that enable multi-step reasoning in large language models, covering both implicit (latent) and explicit (e.g., Chain-of-Thought) reasoning paradigms?
papers.core_contribution: This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the mechanisms underlying multi-step reasoning in large language models, organizing existing research around seven interconnected research questions and highlighting future research directions.
papers.conclusion: The survey concludes by highlighting five open research directions for future mechanistic understanding of multi-step reasoning in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Implicit multi-hop reasoning in LLMs is an orchestrated, layered process with distinct modules specializing in different phases, but it is constrained by the fixed depth of transformers.
Implicit reasoning capability emerges via grokking, a phase transition from memorization to generalization, influenced by training data distribution, data scale, and optimization biases.
LLMs frequently bypass genuine multi-step reasoning by using shortcuts, such as direct input-output associations (factual shortcuts) or surface-level heuristics (structural shortcuts).
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting activates a 'reasoning mode' where models use generated tokens as external memory, breaking the depth limitation and enhancing computational expressiveness and generalization.
CoT does not equate to faithful explainability; it often functions as post-hoc rationalization due to a structural mismatch between the distributed, parallel computation of transformers and the sequential nature of explicit reasoning.
future_direction: Rigorous causal analysis in real-world settings
Bridging the faithfulness gap of explicit CoT reasoning
Mechanistic understanding of Latent CoT reasoning
White-box evaluation metrics for LLM reasoning
From mechanistic interpretation to model control
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable abilities to solve problems requiring multiple reasoning steps, yet the internal mechanisms enabling such capabilities remain elusive. Unlike existing surveys that primarily focus on engineering methods to enhance performance, this survey provides a comprehensive overview of the mechanisms underlying LLM multi-step reasoning. We organize the survey around a conceptual framework comprising seven interconnected research questions, from how LLMs execute implicit multi-hop reasoning within hidden activations to how verbalized explicit reasoning remodels the internal computation. Finally, we highlight five research directions for future mechanistic studies.

papers.title: Not All Neural Embeddings are Born Equal
papers.research_question: How does the architecture/objective function of neural models affect the information encoded in their word embeddings, specifically comparing translation-based and monolingual embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: Translation-based word embeddings outperform monolingual embeddings on tasks requiring knowledge of conceptual similarity and syntactic role, suggesting the translation objective better captures the ontological status of concepts.
papers.conclusion: Neural machine translation models learn word embeddings that more effectively encode conceptual similarity and syntactic role information compared to monolingual models, likely due to the cross-lingual alignment pressure of the translation objective.
papers.key_findings:
Translation-based embeddings achieve higher correlation on SimLex-999 (similarity) and higher accuracy on the TOEFL synonym test and synonym/antonym classification compared to monolingual embeddings.
Monolingual embeddings perform better on relatedness tasks (WordSim-353, MEN).
Translation-based embeddings excel at syntactic analogies, while monolingual embeddings are better at semantic analogies.
The performance advantage of translation-based embeddings on similarity tasks is not due to training data quantity, as monolingual models trained on larger corpora do not match their performance.
The translation objective may induce embeddings that better approximate ontological similarity by aligning words across languages, even when their co-occurrence patterns differ.
papers.abstract: Neural language models learn word representations that capture rich linguistic and conceptual information. Here we investigate the embeddings learned by neural machine translation models. We show that translation-based embeddings outperform those learned by cutting-edge monolingual models at single-language tasks requiring knowledge of conceptual similarity and/or syntactic role. The findings suggest that, while monolingual models learn information about how concepts are related, neural-translation models better capture their true ontological status.

papers.title: Identifying Cooperative Personalities in Multi-agent Contexts through Personality Steering with Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: How do personality traits, steered via representation engineering, affect LLM behavior and cooperation in multi-agent games like the Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma?
papers.core_contribution: Personality steering using representation engineering effectively promotes cooperation in LLM-based multi-agent systems, but with a trade-off between cooperation and vulnerability to exploitation.
papers.conclusion: Personality steering through representation engineering effectively promotes cooperation in LLM-based multi-agent systems, providing a foundation for future work in cooperative AI agents.
papers.key_findings:
Steering towards agreeableness, conscientiousness, and openness reduces troublemaking rates to zero.
High agreeableness increases exploitability, highlighting a trade-off between cooperation and vulnerability.
Agreeableness and conscientiousness lower lying rates, promoting honesty regardless of opponent behavior.
Models steered towards agreeableness and conscientiousness achieve better collective outcomes but worse individual outcomes.
Personality-steered behavior aligns with human psychological traits in similar contexts.
papers.limitation:
Limited to Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma variants and a single payoff matrix.
Effectiveness across different LLM architectures and tasks remains an open question.
Real-world multi-agent interactions involve more complex incentives.
future_direction: Explore diverse game-theoretic frameworks beyond IPD
Validate results across broader contexts and applications
Investigate effectiveness across different LLM architectures
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) gain autonomous capabilities, their coordination in multi-agent settings becomes increasingly important. However, they often struggle with cooperation, leading to suboptimal outcomes. Inspired by Axelrod's Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma (IPD) tournaments, we explore how personality traits influence LLM cooperation. Using representation engineering, we steer Big Five traits (e.g., Agreeableness, Conscientiousness) in LLMs and analyze their impact on IPD decision-making. Our results show that higher Agreeableness and Conscientiousness improve cooperation but increase susceptibility to exploitation, highlighting both the potential and limitations of personality-based steering for aligning AI agents.

papers.title: What Are Large Language Models Mapping to in the Brain? A Case Against Over-Reliance on Brain Scores
papers.research_question: What are large language models mapping to in the brain? The paper questions whether high brain scores indicate shared computational principles between LLMs and human language processing or are explained by simpler, theoretically uninteresting features.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that high brain scores of LLMs on neural datasets can be largely explained by simple features like sentence length, position, and static word embeddings, cautioning against over-interpreting these scores as evidence of shared computational principles with human language processing.
papers.conclusion: Brain scores on the analyzed datasets should be interpreted with caution, and analyses using brain scores should be accompanied by a systematic deconstruction of neural encoding performance against simple features to avoid over-interpretation.
papers.key_findings:
Shuffled train-test splits are severely affected by temporal autocorrelation, and a trivial feature (OASM) that encodes this autocorrelation outperforms LLMs and accounts for most of their explained neural variance.
Untrained GPT2-XL's brain score is fully accounted for by two simple features: sentence length and sentence position.
Trained GPT2-XL's brain score is largely explained by sentence length, sentence position, and static word embeddings; only a small additional amount is explained by sense embeddings and contextual syntactic representations.
On the Fedorenko dataset, word position explains all of the untrained and most of the trained GPT2-XL neural predictivity.
On the Blank dataset, GPT2-XL predicts neural activity at chance levels when using contiguous train-test splits.
papers.limitation:
The method of examining how much neural variance an LLM predicts over simple features scales poorly when the number of feature spaces is large.
The procedure may be biased against regressions with many feature spaces due to noise in neural data and low sample sizes.
The study did not analyze datasets with large amounts of neural data per participant, where the gap between simple and complex features might be larger.
papers.abstract: Given the remarkable capabilities of large language models (LLMs), there has been a growing interest in evaluating their similarity to the human brain. One approach towards quantifying this similarity is by measuring how well a model predicts neural signals, also called "brain score". Internal representations from LLMs achieve state-of-the-art brain scores, leading to speculation that they share computational principles with human language processing. This inference is only valid if the subset of neural activity predicted by LLMs reflects core elements of language processing. Here, we question this assumption by analyzing three neural datasets used in an impactful study on LLM-to-brain mappings, with a particular focus on an fMRI dataset where participants read short passages. We first find that when using shuffled train-test splits, as done in previous studies with these datasets, a trivial feature that encodes temporal autocorrelation not only outperforms LLMs but also accounts for the majority of neural variance that LLMs explain. We therefore use contiguous splits moving forward. Second, we explain the surprisingly high brain scores of untrained LLMs by showing they do not account for additional neural variance beyond two simple features: sentence length and sentence position. This undermines evidence used to claim that the transformer architecture biases computations to be more brain-like. Third, we find that brain scores of trained LLMs on this dataset can largely be explained by sentence length, position, and pronoun-dereferenced static word embeddings; a small, additional amount is explained by sense-specific embeddings and contextual representations of sentence structure. We conclude that over-reliance on brain scores can lead to over-interpretations of similarity between LLMs and brains, and emphasize the importance of deconstructing what LLMs are mapping to in neural signals.

papers.title: Seeking Neural Nuggets: Knowledge Transfer in Large Language Models from a Parametric Perspective
papers.research_question: Whether implicit knowledge stored in the parameters of a larger language model (teacher) can be transferred to a smaller model (student) through a parametric perspective.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a parametric knowledge transfer paradigm that extracts task-specific parameters from a teacher model using sensitivity-based techniques and injects them into a student model via LoRA, demonstrating the transferability of implicit knowledge across LLMs of different scales.
papers.conclusion: Parametric knowledge transfer is feasible and effective; the proposed framework successfully transfers knowledge from larger to smaller LLMs, and the analysis highlights key factors that contribute to successful transfer.
papers.key_findings:
Transferring extracted parameters from a teacher to a student model consistently improves the student's performance across reasoning, professional knowledge, instruction-driven, and open-ended conversation benchmarks.
The structural integrity of the extracted parameters (e.g., preserving submatrices) is crucial for effective transfer, outperforming random or single-weight extraction.
Sensitivity-based parameter extraction outperforms random selection, and the origin of parameters (which modules) matters more than the sheer number of parameters transferred.
Scaling up the teacher model generally leads to better student performance, even when there are architectural differences between models.
The number of seed samples used for sensitivity calculation and the initialization strategy for the LoRA module are important factors influencing transfer efficacy.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) inherently encode a wealth of knowledge within their parameters through pre-training on extensive corpora. While prior research has delved into operations on these parameters to manipulate the underlying implicit knowledge (encompassing detection, editing, and merging), there remains an ambiguous understanding regarding their transferability across models with varying scales. In this paper, we seek to empirically investigate knowledge transfer from larger to smaller models through a parametric perspective. To achieve this, we employ sensitivity-based techniques to extract and align knowledge-specific parameters between different LLMs. Moreover, the LoRA module is used as the intermediary mechanism for injecting the extracted knowledge into smaller models. Evaluations across four benchmarks validate the efficacy of our proposed method. Our findings highlight the critical factors contributing to the process of parametric knowledge transfer, underscoring the transferability of model parameters across LLMs of different scales. Project website: https://maszhongming.github.io/ParaKnowTransfer.

papers.title: LinguaMap: Which Layers of LLMs Speak Your Language and How to Tune Them?
papers.research_question: Where in the model do language-specific behaviors–such as language consistency, dominance bias, and multilingual interference–reside, and can they be isolated to enable efficient and effective multilingual adaptation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework to evaluate language control in multilingual LLMs, reveals a three-phase internal structure (semantic alignment, reasoning, language generation), and proposes selective fine-tuning of the final layers to improve language consistency without sacrificing task performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that layer-localization of language control enables efficient multilingual adaptation via selective fine-tuning, achieving high language consistency with minimal parameter updates.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual LLMs exhibit two key failure modes: the multilingual transfer bottleneck (correct language, incorrect task response) and the language consistency bottleneck (correct task response, wrong language).
Internal analysis using logit lens and hidden state similarity reveals a three-phase structure: early layers align inputs into a shared semantic space, middle layers perform task reasoning, and late layers drive language-specific generation.
Selective fine-tuning of only the final layers responsible for language control achieves over 98% language consistency across six languages while fine-tuning only 3–5% of parameters, matching the performance of full-scope fine-tuning.
The method is effective on models like Qwen-3-32B and Bloom-7.1B, improving language consistency from <20% to 98+% without compromising task accuracy.
Code-switched prompting severely degrades language consistency, highlighting a disconnect between task competence and language control in multilingual LLMs.
papers.abstract: Despite multilingual pretraining, large language models often struggle with non-English tasks, particularly in language control, the ability to respond in the intended language. We identify and characterize two key failure modes: the multilingual transfer bottleneck (correct language, incorrect task response) and the language consistency bottleneck (correct task response, wrong language). To systematically surface these issues, we design a four-scenario evaluation protocol spanning MMLU, MGSM, and XQuAD benchmarks. To probe these issues with interpretability, we extend logit lens analysis to track language probabilities layer by layer and compute cross-lingual semantic similarity of hidden states. The results reveal a three-phase internal structure: early layers align inputs into a shared semantic space, middle layers perform task reasoning, and late layers drive language-specific generation. Guided by these insights, we introduce selective fine-tuning of only the final layers responsible for language control. On Qwen-3-32B and Bloom-7.1B, this method achieves over 98 percent language consistency across six languages while fine-tuning only 3-5 percent of parameters, without sacrificing task accuracy. Importantly, this result is nearly identical to that of full-scope fine-tuning (for example, above 98 percent language consistency for both methods across all prompt scenarios) but uses a fraction of the computational resources. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first approach to leverage layer-localization of language control for efficient multilingual adaptation.

papers.title: Exploring Representational Disparities Between Multilingual and Bilingual Translation Models
papers.research_question: How does the ambient space utilization of model representations differ between bilingual models and one-to-many models? If space utilization differs, what might be driving these differences?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual decoder representations are consistently less isotropic and occupy fewer dimensions than bilingual decoder representations, largely due to language-specific information occupying representational capacity.
papers.conclusion: There is a consistent reduction in representational capacity in multilingual decoders versus bilingual decoders, attributed to language information occupying a significant portion of the representation space.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual decoder representations are less isotropic than bilingual decoder representations across different data resource levels and language pairs.
Multilingual encoder representations are slightly more isotropic than bilingual encoder representations, but the improvement is smaller than the decoder reduction.
The reduction in multilingual decoder isotropy is driven by language-specific information occupying much of the available representation space.
Isotropy decreases with larger training scale, related to the representation degeneration problem.
In multiparallel data, the decoder isotropy reduction is less pronounced for related languages (e.g., Russian and Ukrainian).
papers.limitation:
Models cover at most 3 language families, while modern multilingual translation models cover many more.
Focus on one-to-many models, but many-to-many models may have different behavior.
Focus on encoder-decoder models, but decoder-only translation models may differ.
Work focuses on characterization, not on improving representational capacity.
future_direction: Analyze models with larger language coverage.
Investigate many-to-many multilingual models.
Study decoder-only translation models.
papers.abstract: Multilingual machine translation has proven immensely useful for both parameter efficiency and overall performance across many language pairs via complete multilingual parameter sharing. However, some language pairs in multilingual models can see worse performance than in bilingual models, especially in the one-to-many translation setting. Motivated by their empirical differences, we examine the geometric differences in representations from bilingual models versus those from one-to-many multilingual models. Specifically, we compute the isotropy of these representations using intrinsic dimensionality and IsoScore, in order to measure how the representations utilize the dimensions in their underlying vector space. Using the same evaluation data in both models, we find that for a given language pair, its multilingual model decoder representations are consistently less isotropic and occupy fewer dimensions than comparable bilingual model decoder representations. Additionally, we show that much of the anisotropy in multilingual decoder representations can be attributed to modeling language-specific information, therefore limiting remaining representational capacity.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Large Reasoning Models: A Survey of Training, Inference, and Failures
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that drive the reasoning behaviors and failures of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This survey synthesizes recent research on the mechanistic understanding of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), organizing insights into training dynamics, reasoning mechanisms, and unintended behaviors to bridge the gap between performance and transparency.
papers.conclusion: The survey highlights the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework to advance the mechanistic understanding of LRMs.
papers.key_findings:
SFT expands exploratory paths while RL compresses them, leading to entropy reduction and performance gains.
RL training follows a two-stage process where basic skills are acquired first, followed by the emergence of reasoning abilities.
LRMs exhibit unique reasoning structures, including cyclical processes and topological properties, driven by key behavioral primitives.
Hallucinations in LRMs are influenced by RL, which reduces abstention and can increase incorrect answers.
Chain-of-thought reasoning in LRMs is often unfaithful, with a disconnect between internal states and verbalized traces.
papers.limitation:
The rapid development of LRM research means that new findings may not be captured in this survey.
The survey focuses primarily on language models, excluding multimodal capabilities.
The discussion is limited to traditional LLM architectures, excluding newer approaches like diffusion-based LLMs.
future_direction: Applied interpretability for training-time and inference-time improvements
Development of scalable and generalizable mechanistic interpretability frameworks
Establishment of a unified theoretical framework for reasoning in LRMs
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has catalyzed the emergence of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that have pushed reasoning capabilities to new heights. While their performance has garnered significant excitement, exploring the internal mechanisms driving these behaviors has become an equally critical research frontier. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of the mechanistic understanding of LRMs, organizing recent findings into three core dimensions: 1) training dynamics, 2) reasoning mechanisms, and 3) unintended behaviors. By synthesizing these insights, we aim to bridge the gap between black-box performance and mechanistic transparency. Finally, we discuss under-explored challenges to outline a roadmap for future mechanistic studies, including the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework.

papers.title: Explanations of Large Language Models Explain Language Representations in the Brain
papers.research_question: Are LLM-derived explanations effective in explaining language processing in the brain? Do the observed similarities between LLMs and the brain arise from shared pathways or are they simply artifacts of high-dimensional feature spaces?
papers.core_contribution: Attribution methods from explainable AI (XAI) can robustly predict brain activity during language processing, revealing a hierarchical alignment where early model layers correspond to early brain processing stages and later layers to higher-order stages.
papers.conclusion: XAI methods, particularly attribution, provide a powerful tool for linking LLMs and the brain, revealing shared computational principles for language processing and offering a brain-alignment framework for assessing explanation quality.
papers.key_findings:
Attribution methods (Gradient Norm and Gradient × Input) predict brain activity across the language network, outperforming internal representations (activations, attention) in early language processing regions.
A hierarchical alignment exists: explanations from early LLM layers align with early brain processing areas (e.g., auditory cortex), while later layers align with higher-order areas (e.g., inferior frontal gyrus).
Layers with greater influence on next-word prediction (higher attribution scores) show stronger brain alignment, with a strong correlation between layer importance for prediction and brain alignment.
The predictive capability of attribution methods is consistent across participants and stories, and they encode brain-relevant information in a more compact representation compared to high-dimensional internal representations.
The study positions attribution methods as a powerful tool for bridging LLMs and the brain, offering a novel framework for evaluating XAI methods via neurobiological alignment.
future_direction: Examining a broader range of models, attribution techniques, and brain recording modalities to identify factors shaping alignment.
Extending the brain-explanation alignment approach to other cognitive domains (vision, auditory perception) and multimodal models.
Quantitatively comparing brain-based evaluation frameworks with traditional behavioral evaluation methods for XAI.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) not only exhibit human-like performance but also share computational principles with the brain's language processing mechanisms. While prior research has focused on mapping LLMs' internal representations to neural activity, we propose a novel approach using explainable AI (XAI) to strengthen this link. Applying attribution methods, we quantify the influence of preceding words on LLMs' next-word predictions and use these explanations to predict fMRI data from participants listening to narratives. We find that attribution methods robustly predict brain activity across the language network, revealing a hierarchical pattern: explanations from early layers align with the brain's initial language processing stages, while later layers correspond to more advanced stages. Additionally, layers with greater influence on next-word prediction$\unicode{x2014}$reflected in higher attribution scores$\unicode{x2014}$demonstrate stronger brain alignment. These results underscore XAI's potential for exploring the neural basis of language and suggest brain alignment for assessing the biological plausibility of explanation methods.

papers.title: Data-Centric Interpretability for LLM-based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.research_question: How can we understand behavior changes in LLM-based multi-agent reinforcement learning during training using data-centric interpretability methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Meta-Autointerp, a method for grouping SAE features into interpretable hypotheses about training dynamics, and shows that SAEs and LLM-summarizer provide complementary views into agent behavior in multi-agent RL.
papers.conclusion: The framework combining SAEs and LLM-summarizer provides complementary views into agent behavior and is a practical starting point for data-centric interpretability in multi-agent RL.
papers.key_findings:
SAE Meta-Features (grouped features) are more interpretable and predictively useful than individual SAE features.
LLM summarizer hypotheses are subjectively interesting but less predictively useful than SAE-derived hypotheses.
The framework discovers fine-grained behaviors (e.g., role-playing, language switching) and high-level strategic behaviors in multi-agent RL training.
A subset of SAE-derived hypotheses are predictively useful for downstream tasks, such as distinguishing early vs late training samples.
Hypotheses from SAE Meta-Features can be used to improve agent performance via prompt optimization, achieving a +14.2% score improvement.
papers.limitation:
Subjectively interesting SAE features and most LLM generated hypotheses may be worse than useless to humans.
Sparsity of feature activations is a major limitation, making some features subtle and difficult for humans to distinguish.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly trained in complex Reinforcement Learning, multi-agent environments, making it difficult to understand how behavior changes over training. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have recently shown to be useful for data-centric interpretability. In this work, we analyze large-scale reinforcement learning training runs from the sophisticated environment of Full-Press Diplomacy by applying pretrained SAEs, alongside LLM-summarizer methods. We introduce Meta-Autointerp, a method for grouping SAE features into interpretable hypotheses about training dynamics. We discover fine-grained behaviors including role-playing patterns, degenerate outputs, language switching, alongside high-level strategic behaviors and environment-specific bugs. Through automated evaluation, we validate that 90% of discovered SAE Meta-Features are significant, and find a surprising reward hacking behavior. However, through two user studies, we find that even subjectively interesting and seemingly helpful SAE features may be worse than useless to humans, along with most LLM generated hypotheses. However, a subset of SAE-derived hypotheses are predictively useful for downstream tasks. We further provide validation by augmenting an untrained agent's system prompt, improving the score by +14.2%. Overall, we show that SAEs and LLM-summarizer provide complementary views into agent behavior, and together our framework forms a practical starting point for future data-centric interpretability work on ensuring trustworthy LLM behavior throughout training.

papers.title: Revisiting Modality Invariance in a Multilingual Speech-Text Model via Neuron-Level Analysis
papers.research_question: How and when do multilingual speech–text models reuse shared circuitry across modalities, and how does this reuse differ between input-language representation and output-language generation during decoding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a generation-step-aware framework for cross-modal evaluation of multilingual speech-text models, revealing that cross-modal language alignment is time- and function-dependent, with representation alignment strongest at early steps and control alignment strengthening later.
papers.conclusion: Cross-modal processing in multilingual speech-text models is both time-dependent and function-dependent, highlighting the importance of generation-aware diagnostics for evaluating multilingual behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Cross-modal language alignment for language-representation neurons is strongest at the first decoding step but weakens as generation proceeds, indicating a shift from shared to modality-specific processing.
Language-control neurons identified from speech transfer causally to text generation, revealing partially shared circuitry for output-language control.
The cross-modal effect ratio for language control increases at later decoding steps, showing stronger transfer of control mechanisms.
The distribution of language-selective neurons shifts from self-attention to cross-attention as decoding proceeds, indicating a transition from encoder-driven to autoregressive processing.
Cross-modal neuron overlap shows a strong diagonal (same-language) preference at the first step, which weakens at later steps.
papers.limitation:
Focus on a single model architecture (SeamlessM4T v2).
Reliance on AP-based neuron identification, which captures statistical associations but does not establish causal necessity.
Use of synthetic speech to control for acoustic variability, which may not fully reflect natural speech.
Asymmetries across tasks (e.g., ASR vs. text repetition) and language tags might introduce noise in neuron identification and cross-modal comparisons.
future_direction: Verify whether similar patterns hold for natural speech.
Explore more symmetric settings, such as En→X translation across modalities.
papers.abstract: Multilingual speech-text foundation models aim to process language uniformly across both modality and language, yet it remains unclear whether they internally represent the same language consistently when it is spoken versus written. We investigate this question in SeamlessM4T v2 through three complementary analyses that probe where language and modality information is encoded, how selective neurons causally influence decoding, and how concentrated this influence is across the network. We identify language- and modality-selective neurons using average-precision ranking, investigate their functional role via median-replacement interventions at inference time, and analyze activation-magnitude inequality across languages and modalities. Across experiments, we find evidence of incomplete modality invariance. Although encoder representations become increasingly language-agnostic, this compression makes it more difficult for the shared decoder to recover the language of origin when constructing modality-agnostic representations, particularly when adapting from speech to text. We further observe sharply localized modality-selective structure in cross-attention key and value projections. Finally, speech-conditioned decoding and non-dominant scripts exhibit higher activation concentration, indicating heavier reliance on a small subset of neurons, which may underlie increased brittleness across modalities and languages.

papers.title: Large Language Models Are Human-Like Internally
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether surprisal (negative log probability) from internal layers of large language models aligns with human sentence processing data, and whether the alignment varies by layer depth and the type of human measure (behavioral vs. neurophysiological).
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that surprisal from internal layers of larger language models aligns well with human sentence processing data, challenging prior conclusions that focused on final layers. Additionally, it finds that earlier layers align with fast human measures (e.g., gaze duration) and later layers with slower measures (e.g., N400).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that larger language models are cognitively plausible when internal layers are considered, and that different layers correspond to different stages of human sentence processing, advocating for layer-wise alignment in cognitive modeling.
papers.key_findings:
Surprisal from internal layers of larger LMs aligns with human sentence processing data as well as or better than smaller LMs.
The last layer does not yield the best alignment; the best layer varies by human measure.
Earlier layers align better with fast human measures (e.g., first-pass gaze duration, self-paced reading time), while later layers align better with slower measures (e.g., N400, MAZE processing time).
When considering the best internal layer, larger LMs show a positive scaling effect (larger models have higher ∆LL) for most human measures.
The alignment patterns are consistent across multiple languages (tested on MECO corpus).
papers.limitation: The study is focused on naturalistic reading corpora and does not include controlled experiments on syntactic ambiguity or grammatical violation, which are known challenges for surprisal theory.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other probability-based measures such as entropy and entropy reduction.
Combine the internal layer approach with linguistically-motivated neural models.
papers.abstract: Recent cognitive modeling studies have reported that larger language models (LMs) exhibit a poorer fit to human reading behavior (Oh and Schuler, 2023b; Shain et al., 2024; Kuribayashi et al., 2024), leading to claims of their cognitive implausibility. In this paper, we revisit this argument through the lens of mechanistic interpretability and argue that prior conclusions were skewed by an exclusive focus on the final layers of LMs. Our analysis reveals that next-word probabilities derived from internal layers of larger LMs align with human sentence processing data as well as, or better than, those from smaller LMs. This alignment holds consistently across behavioral (self-paced reading times, gaze durations, MAZE task processing times) and neurophysiological (N400 brain potentials) measures, challenging earlier mixed results and suggesting that the cognitive plausibility of larger LMs has been underestimated. Furthermore, we first identify an intriguing relationship between LM layers and human measures: earlier layers correspond more closely with fast gaze durations, while later layers better align with relatively slower signals such as N400 potentials and MAZE processing times. Our work opens new avenues for interdisciplinary research at the intersection of mechanistic interpretability and cognitive modeling.

papers.title: Inducing Systematicity in Transformers by Attending to Structurally Quantized Embeddings
papers.research_question: How to induce systematicity in Transformers with low-complexity training data to improve compositional generalization?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SQ-Transformer, which uses Structure-oriented Vector Quantization (SoVQ) and systematic attention layers (SAL/SRL) to induce systematicity and improve compositional generalization in Transformers.
papers.conclusion: SQ-Transformer effectively induces systematicity in Transformers and improves compositional generalization, providing insights into the inner mechanisms of Transformers and laying groundwork for future architecture design.
papers.key_findings:
SQ-Transformer achieves stronger compositional generalization than vanilla Transformer on multiple low-complexity semantic parsing and machine translation datasets.
SoVQ learns a syntactically clustered embedding space.
SAL/SRL induce generalizable attention patterns that lead to improved systematicity.
SQ-Transformer with SAL works well on small synthetic datasets, while SRL is better for larger natural datasets.
The method is effective even without data augmentation or large pretraining.
papers.limitation: SQ-Transformer does not explicitly encourage phrasal constituents with the same syntactic role to be close in representation space, limiting performance on deeper recursion and novel combinations of grammatical structures and phrasal constituents.
future_direction: Handling phrasal constituents and deeper recursion in compositional generalization.
papers.abstract: Transformers generalize to novel compositions of structures and entities after being trained on a complex dataset, but easily overfit on datasets of insufficient complexity. We observe that when the training set is sufficiently complex, the model encodes sentences that have a common syntactic structure using a systematic attention pattern. Inspired by this observation, we propose SQ-Transformer (Structurally Quantized) that explicitly encourages systematicity in the embeddings and attention layers, even with a training set of low complexity. At the embedding level, we introduce Structure-oriented Vector Quantization (SoVQ) to cluster word embeddings into several classes of structurally equivalent entities. At the attention level, we devise the Systematic Attention Layer (SAL) and an alternative, Systematically Regularized Layer (SRL) that operate on the quantized word embeddings so that sentences of the same structure are encoded with invariant or similar attention patterns. Empirically, we show that SQ-Transformer achieves stronger compositional generalization than the vanilla Transformer on multiple low-complexity semantic parsing and machine translation datasets. In our analysis, we show that SoVQ indeed learns a syntactically clustered embedding space and SAL/SRL induces generalizable attention patterns, which lead to improved systematicity.

papers.title: Neuron-Level Analysis of Cultural Understanding in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the existence and distribution of culture-general and culture-specific neurons in LLMs? How do these neurons contribute to cultural understanding and what are their potential engineering applications?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces CULNIG, a gradient-based method to identify culture-general and culture-specific neurons in LLMs. It finds that these neurons are few (<1% of all neurons) and concentrated in shallow to middle MLP layers, and that suppressing them significantly degrades cultural understanding while minimally affecting general NLU tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that culture-general and culture-specific neurons exist in LLMs and play a crucial role in cultural understanding. The findings provide insights into the internal mechanisms of LLMs and offer practical guidance for model training and engineering.
papers.key_findings:
Culture-general and culture-specific neurons account for less than 1% of all neurons and are concentrated in shallow to middle MLP layers.
Suppressing culture-general neurons substantially degrades performance on cultural benchmarks (by up to 30%) while performance on general NLU benchmarks remains largely unaffected.
Culture-specific neurons support knowledge of not only the target culture but also related cultures.
Training on NLU benchmarks can diminish models' cultural understanding when updating modules containing many culture-general neurons.
The gradient-based attribution method (CULNIG) effectively identifies neurons that contribute to cultural understanding.
future_direction: Further investigation of the discrepancy between CULNIG and CAPE neuron distributions
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed worldwide, ensuring their fair and comprehensive cultural understanding is important. However, LLMs exhibit cultural bias and limited awareness of underrepresented cultures, while the mechanisms underlying their cultural understanding remain underexplored. To fill this gap, we conduct a neuron-level analysis to identify neurons that drive cultural behavior, introducing a gradient-based scoring method with additional filtering for precise refinement. We identify both culture-general neurons contributing to cultural understanding regardless of cultures, and culture-specific neurons tied to an individual culture. These neurons account for less than 1% of all neurons and are concentrated in shallow to middle MLP layers. We validate their role by showing that suppressing them substantially degrades performance on cultural benchmarks (by up to 30%), while performance on general natural language understanding (NLU) benchmarks remains largely unaffected. Moreover, we show that culture-specific neurons support knowledge of not only the target culture, but also related cultures. Finally, we demonstrate that training on NLU benchmarks can diminish models' cultural understanding when we update modules containing many culture-general neurons. These findings provide insights into the internal mechanisms of LLMs and offer practical guidance for model training and engineering. Our code is available at https://github.com/ynklab/CULNIG

papers.title: The Clock and the Pizza: Two Stories in Mechanistic Explanation of Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Do neural networks, trained on well-understood algorithmic tasks, reliably re-discover known algorithms for solving those tasks, and under what conditions do they discover familiar algorithmic solutions?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks trained on modular addition can discover qualitatively different algorithms (Clock, Pizza, and others), with the algorithm learned depending on hyperparameters like attention rate and width, revealing algorithmic phase transitions and the need for tools to characterize algorithmic phase spaces.
papers.conclusion: Algorithmic discoveries in neural networks are not inevitable; even simple tasks admit a diversity of solutions, motivating the development of tools to characterize the algorithmic phase space of neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Networks can learn either the previously described Clock algorithm or a new, less intuitive Pizza algorithm for modular addition.
The Pizza algorithm uses averaging and absolute value operations, while the Clock algorithm uses multiplication via attention.
Models sometimes implement multiple, parallel copies of an algorithm (ensembling) for robustness.
Sharp algorithmic phase transitions between Clock and Pizza occur as model hyperparameters (attention rate, width) are varied.
Non-circular algorithms also exist, especially in deeper networks or with low attention rates.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on a single learning problem (modular addition), and scaling the techniques to more complex models and real-world tasks requires significant additional work.
future_direction: How to find, classify, and interpret unfamiliar algorithms in a systematic way.
How to disentangle multiple, parallel algorithm implementations in the presence of ensembling.
papers.abstract: Do neural networks, trained on well-understood algorithmic tasks, reliably rediscover known algorithms for solving those tasks? Several recent studies, on tasks ranging from group arithmetic to in-context linear regression, have suggested that the answer is yes. Using modular addition as a prototypical problem, we show that algorithm discovery in neural networks is sometimes more complex. Small changes to model hyperparameters and initializations can induce the discovery of qualitatively different algorithms from a fixed training set, and even parallel implementations of multiple such algorithms. Some networks trained to perform modular addition implement a familiar Clock algorithm; others implement a previously undescribed, less intuitive, but comprehensible procedure which we term the Pizza algorithm, or a variety of even more complex procedures. Our results show that even simple learning problems can admit a surprising diversity of solutions, motivating the development of new tools for characterizing the behavior of neural networks across their algorithmic phase space.

papers.title: Demystifying the Roles of LLM Layers in Retrieval, Knowledge, and Reasoning
papers.research_question: How can we rigorously evaluate the contribution of each layer to overall LLM performance under different evaluation protocols?
papers.core_contribution: The paper systematically shows that depth usage in LLMs is highly heterogeneous and context-dependent, with shallow layers dominating likelihood and retrieval tasks, while middle and deeper layers are crucial for reasoning and generation.
papers.conclusion: Results show that layer contributions are highly uneven: shallow layers dominate likelihood and retrieval, while mid-to-deep layers are essential for reasoning and generation. Depth usage is inherently task-dependent, highly metric-sensitive, and strongly model-specific, highlighting the critical need for task-aware evaluation and offering practical guidance for compression and future model design.
papers.key_findings:
Under likelihood-based metrics, pruning most layers preserves performance, with only initial layers being critical; generation-based evaluation shows middle and deeper layers are indispensable for reasoning and long-range coherence.
Knowledge and retrieval are concentrated in shallow components, with removal of early layers causing sharp degradation in retrieval tasks.
Reasoning accuracy relies heavily on deeper layers and is more sensitive to ablation in middle and deep layers.
Distillation not only improves baseline accuracy but also redistributes reasoning capacity more evenly across depth, enhancing robustness under ablation.
Retrieval and reasoning abilities are localized to specific attention heads rather than being uniformly distributed.
papers.abstract: Recent studies suggest that the deeper layers of Large Language Models (LLMs) contribute little to representation learning and can often be removed without significant performance loss. However, such claims are typically drawn from narrow evaluations and may overlook important aspects of model behavior. In this work, we present a systematic study of depth utilization across diverse dimensions, including evaluation protocols, task categories, and model architectures.
